This research focuses on the analysis of a stochastic control problem governed by a parabolic equation with a specific type of control appearing in the diffusion term. We first establish the existence of an optimal control solution within a strong control space, then prove that this solution is unique when the control space is strengthened. We also demonstrate the differentiability of the state map and establish regularity results for the state and the cost functional. Furthermore, we show that the adjoint system comprises the Laplace operator applied to the gradient of an unknown function, multiplied by a stochastic convolution operator, and we establish the boundedness of the admissibility operator and the differentiability of the algebraic operator. Finally, we provide an application to a stochastic version of the Oberbeck-Binswanger problem. This research extends previous findings, as it generalizes the results obtained in two specific cases. Additionally, it provides new insights into the Oberbeck-Binswanger problem. Systematic use is made of the techniques of stochastic functional analysis, particularly the theory of operator-valued Ricard-type holomorphic families, which is presented in an appendix as part of the underlying framework. Our comprehensive study of 31 extremely energetic cosmic rays, surpassing 8 EeV in energy, reveals a distinct pattern of behavior. These particles, detected by the HiRes experiment at the Fermilab National Accelerator Laboratory, exhibit a specific arrival direction distribution that contradicts random chance occurrences. With only one possible explanation, these particles must have originated from a fixed, focused source of high-energy radiation within our galaxy's neighborhood. This discovery challenges previous theories suggesting that cosmic rays above this energy level behave randomly and are likely produced by high-energy neutron stars or black holes. This finding's implications are further explored in a companion paper. Our research examined the fluctuations of the angle and magnitude of particle flows with respect to the collision axis in heavy-ion collisions at the LHC. For lead-lead collisions at 2.76 TeV and 5.02 TeV, and for Xe-Xe collisions at 5.44 TeV, we found significant positive correlations between the fluctuations of the flow angle and magnitude at low transverse momentum. Additionally, we identified the multiplicity dependence of integrated four-particle cumulant correlations related to flow fluctuations, and our results are consistent with previous observations indicating that the properties of heavy-ion collisions are similar in both directions of pseudorapidity. As for the charged-hadron differential distributions of four-particle cumulant correlations related to flow fluctuations, our study shows they conform to the pattern expected from hydrodynamical flow, and allow us to extract the kinetic freeze-out density and velocity relative to the speed of light. As a byproduct, we also obtained the charged-particle pseudorapidity density distributions for minimum-bias collision selections, and the mid-pseudorapidity charged-hadron multiplicity distributions for various collision energies. Lastly, our research includes optimized settings for the flow angle and magnitude fluctuations analysis in the HEP-FlowMap package. This research focuses on addressing inconsistencies in data tables that contain missing values and functional relationships. Unlike conventional approaches that rely on primary keys and foreign keys, our method leverages functional dependencies to identify and rectify inconsistencies. We then develop an algorithm to modify missing values based on the available data. Furthermore, we introduce an indicator to distinguish between explicitly missing and present data. This distinction enables us to reevaluate data quality characteristics. We demonstrate the limitations of this approach by examining certain FD properties and provide examples of data tables to illustrate the method's applicability. Additionally, we outline potential uses of this approach in various applications, including data cleansing, query processing, and data summarization. Moreover, we outline potential extensions to our method, including handling inconsistent data in relational databases and exploring its connection to inconsistent queries. This research lays the groundwork for further investigation into resolving inconsistencies in tables and evaluating data quality characteristics. This paper introduces a time-varying econometric model for count time series data, which applies dynamic generalized linear models and focuses on capturing changes over time in model parameters. We develop a nonparametric approach to estimate the time-varying mean function, using a large number of small time intervals and a high sampling rate. The consistency of the time-varying parameter estimator is proven under certain conditions, and we also establish the asymptotic distribution of the difference of functionals of these estimates. Furthermore, the paper discusses two applications of this research: one is a time-varying version of the Sarafianos et al. model that analyzes the spread of COVID-19, and the other is a time-varying Poisson regression model used to analyze the daily number of new mobile phone users in South Korea. Numerical examples and data analyses demonstrate the effectiveness and versatility of the time-varying econometric model. The associated R package, tvEconometrics, is also introduced, which facilitates the implementation of these models in practical settings.

We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that
replicates both object points and relative transformations, using a unified
framework inspired by descriptor fields. We demonstrate the versatility of NDFs
by applying it to two distinct object manipulation tasks: free-form object
deformation and object-to-target registration. In both applications, we use a
SE(3)-equivariant architecture that leverages the inherent symmetry of NDFs to
predict desired transformation descriptors. These descriptors are then used as
targets to compute the optimal transformation for object points. Experimentally,
we find that NDFs excel in both tasks, surpassing the performance of
state-of-the-art methods. In particular, our results show that NDFs achieve the
lowest reconstruction error in a challenging object synthesis task based on
3D-MNIST. We also provide a code implementation of our approach at the

In statistics and machine learning, it's often crucial to understand how optimization methods navigate non-convex functions. For many applications, researchers have established that, under specific conditions, various methods, such as the empirical risk minimization, enjoy a key property called local convexity. This property ensures that around the optimal solution, the function in question behaves in a convex manner. In this study, we explore how this local convexity affects the theoretical guarantees of optimization methods. Specifically, we examine how it impacts the bounds on solution accuracy when using different methods, focusing on general convex optimization techniques. Our analysis is then applied to establishing performance guarantees for several popular methods used in classification problems. Ultimately, our findings provide a framework for deriving solution quality bounds in the presence of local convexity. This framework can be seen as an extension to the existing results on the sample complexity of model selection, as it allows us to consider more general function classes, including those that are neither finite nor compositional. Our research also introduces a novel measure of function complexity that is well-suited for handling data-dependent quantities, such as empirical risk. We demonstrate the practical utility of this measure by applying it to a classification problem involving neural networks. Our results in this example align with the established findings from the field of neural network learning. We believe that our research on function complexity will be valuable for its own sake, as it provides a theoretical framework that can be used to interpret existing results and aid in the development of new algorithms and models. Our work is also an invitation to the machine learning community to explore the concept of function complexity further, with the aim of making it a more versatile and powerful tool for guiding the design of machine learning models and algorithms. Systematically, we outline the potential directions for future research in this area. Our study is built on the foundation established by the research of Chambertoft et al., specifically their discovery that the expected loss of the empirical risk minimization is bounded by the sum of the maximum expected risk and the complexity of the function class, multiplied by a constant factor that depends on the number of samples. We acknowledge the significant contribution of Chambertoft et al. for providing the initial framework for our research. We also draw inspiration from the related works on the sample complexity of model selection, as well as the research on the PAC-Bayes risk bound, which was first introduced by McAllester, and later expanded upon by Catoni, by Giaccolo and Villa, and by Germain, Seldin, and Jonasson. Accurate and highly precise measurements of the aerosol optical depth in the vertical direction are crucial for assessing the impact of space-based telescopes and photometric systems, but have been challenging to achieve using photometric data from stars. A new method has been developed to determine the aerosol optical depth at a specific altitude using photometric measurements of a single star, and has been applied to data from the Kepler space telescope. This method leverages a new parameterization of the scattering phase function, accounts for uncertainties in the optical properties of aerosols, and utilizes extensive calibration based on ground measurements from AERONET. Following this calibration, the aerosol optical depth at the Earth's surface was estimated using a look-up table, and the results were compared with contemporaneous AERONET measurements at 18 sites with suitable conditions, yielding a mean difference of $0.015\pm0.007$ and a standard deviation of $0.021$. The effectiveness of this method has been demonstrated over an 11-year period for a wide range of conditions, and the associated code is freely available online. The application of this method to photometric time series promises valuable insights into global and long-term variations in aerosol distributions. The limitations of this approach are also discussed, particularly the difficulty in distinguishing between aerosols and tropospheric and stratospheric clouds. Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. This research area can be divided into two primary approaches: regression-based and ranking-based methods. In the latter category, learning a score function to distinguish between potential 2D-3D correspondences is explored. We present a novel, rank-based method that employs a CNN to identify a set of maximum matching correspondences between an input image and a 3D model, which we refer to as the "object part graph". Our algorithm iteratively selects the most likely correspondences by evaluating the consistency between projected control points and local image features. This approach allows us to integrate various descriptors and control point projection operators into a unified framework. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by achieving the current state-of-the-art results in the LPD2015 and Market-36M datasets. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/zhanglei1993/obj_part_graph.

We introduce Generalized Graphical Lasso (GGLasso), a statistical model that incorporates multiple graphs to analyze separable and representable coupling models. Coupling models are then represented as sparse differences of base models specified by the multiple graphs. Our method optimizes a decomposition that minimizes both the $l_1$ norm of the sparsity pattern and the $l_1$ norm of the coupling vectors. This is achieved through an augmented Lagrangian method that utilizes the Graphical Lasso scheme and yields consistent and root-n estimators for the optimal solution. This approach is particularly useful for modeling and inferring hidden structures within coupling models. As an illustration, we apply GGLasso to reconstruct a brain connectivity dynamic that varies over the day. This research is an extension of the static Graphical Lasso developed by Friedman, Hastie, Kisch, and Tibshirani, and the vector-valued sparse model introduced by Yuan and Lin. We also discuss connections to other generalized models including the Group Lasso, Vector Lasso, and the Fused Lasso. The code for GGLasso is available at https://www.jstatsoft.org/index.php/EarlyView. A real-world brain connectivity dynamic network inference example is provided in the supplementary materials available at https://www.jstatsoft.org/vindex.php/GGLasso. Our new method calculates a variation of eigenvector centrality for multi-layered networks that incorporate node importance across different layers. In these networks, defined by separate interconnected graphs without connections between different layers, the value of a node's centrality is determined by the sum of the values of the connected nodes within each specific layer, similar to traditional eigenvector centrality calculations. Unlike standard approaches, our approach takes into account the relationships between different network layers and their respective impact on the centrality values. Unlike current multi-layer eigenvector centrality frameworks that account for inter-layer connections, our approach uses a separate set of equations that can be solved using a hybrid algorithm. Our approach has practical uses in identifying influential nodes within complex, multi-faceted systems such as social media platforms, financial networks, and web graphs. Our algorithm was tested on multiple random multi-layer networks and a well-known collaboration network. The results show that our approach accurately reflects the true values of node centrality according to various metrics. The algorithm's efficiency was found to be linear with respect to the number of nodes and layers in the network. The development of our approach also led to the creation of a new measure for evaluating network layer integration, which was found to be closely related to the distribution of node centrality values across different layers. The algorithm and associated data are available online. The associated measures can be applied to various networks and configurations available on the web. The code is available at https://github.com/ahmadagha/evec_multilayer. The network data is available at https://www.dropbox.

This study investigates the surface seal stage of water impacted by a sphere, focusing on the transition from the surface seal to the jet formation stage. This research examines the properties of a specific type of crystal surface, a (110) surface, and how its behavior changes when the electronic lattice is distorted. A key feature of these lattices is the presence of Dirac cones in their band structure. However, on a (110) surface, the cone's symmetry is broken due to the orientation, leading to the formation of two distinct types of electrons with different mobility: one type, known as the "Dirac electron," is highly mobile and resides at the surface, while the other type, the "heavy hole," remains at the bulk and has limited mobility. When the electronic lattice is altered, either spontaneously or through an external stimulus, the surface's band structure changes, potentially causing the surface to become a semiconductor rather than a metal. This phenomenon can be influenced by the presence of a third dimension, either through the inclusion of a third atomic plane or in the form of an external potential, and may be observable in experiments conducted on surface layers of materials like silicene, phosphorene, and graphene. This research demonstrates that even a two-dimensional crystal surface can behave as a one-dimensional metal at very low temperatures, exhibiting unique characteristics that could be leveraged in the development of superconducting materials. This phenomenon arises specifically from the unique properties of the (110) surface of a two-dimensional electronic lattice. This discovery may also be relevant to the study of materials with one-dimensional electronic properties, such as carbon nanotubes and atomic chains, and could potentially guide experimental research aimed at creating and studying these materials. The associated theoretical framework provides a foundation for exploring entanglement in various continuous-variable systems. The associated analysis reveals that the required storage time to prevent state collapse can be significantly shortened by utilizing a kind of decoy dark storage. The study of these states and the associated theoretical framework can facilitate development of reliable and robust continuous-variable quantum technologies. Tumors within the esophagus are challenging to define manually in CT scans due to their vague boundaries and the presence of air-filled structures within the esophagus. Artificial intelligence can improve the accuracy of tumor boundary identification by using a layer that accounts for the likelihood of pixels belonging to the wall of the esophagus. However, this approach has limitations when dealing with structures within the esophagus that are filled with air, as it can lead to confusion between these structures and tumors. A new strategy has been developed to address this issue by utilizing a U-Net architecture that incorporates features from CT images and probability maps of structures within the esophagus, in addition to likelihood maps of the esophageal wall. This approach enables the creation of a dataset that can be used to train a separate network for tumor segmentation, resulting in a more accurate and efficient method for modeling the complex relationships within the esophagus. Experimental validation revealed that this method can effectively reduce the size of training data required for tumor segmentation tasks by 10-fold, while achieving comparable results to the original method. Furthermore, this approach can be applied to various organs with complex internal structures. This dataset includes corresponding manual delineations and clinical annotations, in addition to segmentation results produced using this method. Cross-domain recommendation has been a significant area of research in the field of Recommender Systems, as it enables effective product recommendations across different platforms for the same user base. Existing cross-domain methods typically focus on integrating data from multiple domains, yet often overlook the presence of multiple sparse domains with different data availability. In contrast, a new approach called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) is proposed to address this issue by developing a framework that accounts for the varying levels of data sparsity across domains. This is achieved through a novel co-factorization framework that combines domain-specific and cross-domain factorization to capture both local and global patterns in the data. Theoretical analysis of the proposed method reveals its optimality conditions, while experimental evaluations on six real-world datasets demonstrate the superior performance of MSDCR over traditional cross-domain methods and alternative sparse-domain baselines. Furthermore, the proposed method is found to be scalable and efficient in practice. To facilitate future research, the code for MSDCR is made publicly available. This work's findings are expected to contribute to a better understanding of cross-domain recommendations in the presence of multiple sparse domains. Convex optimization issues often take on a more manageable form when represented with conic formulations that leverage a wide range of exotic cones. Exotic cones in this context, refer to specialized geometric shapes with properties enabling efficient implementation of computational tools, specifically barrier oracles for their own and dual shapes. This work introduces Hypatia, an interior-point solver designed to handle these complex shapes with ease, allowing for the use of generic exotic cones. Hypatia's flexibility is demonstrated through the resolution of two distinct optimization problems: the first involving the local minimum of a function subject to constraints defined by the convex-envelope cone, and the second, a linear optimization problem for a cone constructed from a set of non-negative, separable functions. Notably, this latter problem can be reconfigured to represent a wide range of well-known exotic cones, including the tensor train cone and the block-structured cone. Hypatia's performance is evaluated through computational experiments using real-world datasets. The resulting solver is available as an open-source tool.

The Motivation Dynamics framework, a concept explored in recent studies that applies bifurcations to model an autonomous agent's decision-making processes, is further developed to accommodate multiple autonomous entities in this paper. We demonstrate how the framework's capabilities can be expanded to capture persistent, cooperative behavior between agents meeting at specific locations, and through in-depth analysis and numerical data, show that this extension exhibits a complex pattern indicative of a strange attractor. Furthermore, our findings reveal that even when one of the autonomous entities malfunctions and alters its meeting location, the stable pattern of meetings can be restored following a period of instability, as the system undergos a supercritical Neimyman bifurcation. Notably, this research reveals that the meeting locations that result from the bifurcation do not return to their original state, and instead settle on the location that was introduced by the faulty agent, providing insight into how small changes in an autonomous system's dynamics can lead to significant and lasting consequences. This study is relevant to various real-world applications, including the analysis of changes to meeting patterns among autonomous drones, and the behavior of populations of birds and insects that migrate to specific locations. The concept of ordered generating sequences (OGS) extends a fundamental property of finite abelian groups to non-abelian groups, providing a distinct generalization. According to its definition, any element within a group can be expressed as a product of various generator powers, arranged in a specific order. For the symmetric group Sn, we establish a structured framework for ordered generating sequences, incorporating permutations that transpose specific positions, and show that each sequence corresponds to a unique Coxeter system. Furthermore, we establish that any sequence is equivalent to another if and only if the corresponding groups generated by those sequences are congruent. Additionally, we demonstrate that the ordered generating sequences for the symmetric group Sn are isotonic, yielding a chain with a height equivalent to the number of pairs of positions that can be transposed, totaling n(n-1)/2. Consequently, we obtain evidence supporting the conjectured coherence of the Coxeter system associated with the symmetric group Sn. As a related finding, we show that the length of the longest chain within this structured framework for the symmetric group Sn is $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor + \lfloor (n-1)/2 \rfloor$. Lastly, we outline a strategy for extending our analysis to finite Coxeter systems. The research presented in this paper is part of a broader dissertation exploring ordered generating sequences for finite groups, Coxeter systems, and related geometric and combinatorial topics. The findings reported here were initially presented at the Group Theory Day, held in honor of A. Shalev's 60th birthday. The algorithm used to determine the ordered generating sequences for the symmetric group Sn was inspired by an approach developed by E. P. O'Brien. The structure of the ordered generating sequences for the symmetric group Sn was also explored in a paper co-authored with M. D. Halls. We investigate the impact of weak lensing from dark matter halos on the observed magnitudes of Type Ia supernovae, considering various dark matter models and the distribution of supernovae within the dark matter field. Using an improved method to calculate the weak lensing effects on the supernova's light, we find that the influence of this effect on the supernova's magnitude is approximately $0.00042$ mag, which is a negligible contribution for current SN Ia datasets but may become significant for future large-scale surveys. We also examine the correlation between the supernova's position, the surrounding mass density, and the weak lensing effect, finding that this correlation could be misinterpreted as being caused by the supernova-progenitor-mass relation. Furthermore, we discuss the limitations of our model, particularly the assumption of a fixed mass-to-light ratio for dark matter halos, and potential future directions, including incorporating more realistic mass distributions and accounting for the non-uniform distribution of supernovae within dark matter halos. We conclude that the impact of weak lensing on SN Ia magnitudes is a crucial consideration for high-precision cosmology, and that future large-scale SN Ia datasets will require more sophisticated models of this effect.

The development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks will heavily rely on reliable creation and management of solid-state devices that interface photons with electronic spins. In silicon material, T-type damage centers exhibit exceptional optical properties and may serve as a suitable photon-spin interface, but until now, it has been extremely difficult to create these centers consistently. Our research presents a method for controlled production of T-type damage centers within silicon wafers, using a simultaneous annealing and etching process that allows for both creation and positioning of these centers at the surface of the material. This breakthrough enables the development of efficient silicon-based devices that interface photons with electronic spins, using a 4 GHz CMOS analog circuit as an example. Our findings demonstrate the ability to position T-type damage centers within a range of 0 to 1 micron below the surface of the silicon, and show that these centers can be used to create a reliable and efficient connection between a microwave circuit and a light source. Our results also reveal that these centers can be used to create a device that can convert a microwave signal into a quantized optical output, demonstrating a potential application in randomized quantum memory. Notably, our method can be integrated into existing silicon photonic chip manufacturing processes. A significant barrier to kidney transplantation arises from the incompatibility between donors and recipients, leading to desensitization protocols for overcoming immunological obstacles. Despite advances in these methods, patients who undergo incompatible transplants face a heightened risk of transplant rejection and require lifelong immunosuppressive treatment. An alternative approach, kidney paired donation, enables the exchange of incompatible patients with suitable matches from other donor recipient pairs, thus providing a compatible transplant for both parties involved. This study aims to evaluate the effectiveness of kidney paired donation in addressing incompatibility issues, specifically focusing on ABO blood type and human leukocyte antigen (HLA) mismatches. An algorithm was developed to maximize the number of compatible transplants within a given pool of potential donors and recipients, taking into account various factors such as blood type, HLA antigen, existing relationships, and waiting time. Using real-world data from 1622 incompatible patients in need of a kidney transplant, the results showed that it is possible to find a match for 44.7% of these patients, with 5.1% being able to participate in multiple exchanges of pairs. Notably, the chances of finding a match increase as more incompatible pairs become available, with 10% of the patients having a 20% chance of being matched with at least one compatible pair. Furthermore, the study highlights the benefits of collaborating with multiple transplant centers and the importance of prioritizing patients with the narrowest range of acceptable HLA antigens. In conclusion, this study demonstrates the effectiveness of kidney paired donation in addressing incompatibility issues and highlights the potential benefits of a centralized national exchange system. Such a system would allow for the coordination of multiple transplant centers, facilitating the exchange of pairs and increasing the chances of finding a compatible match for patients in need of a kidney transplant. In the United States alone, it is estimated that a national exchange system could provide a kidney transplant to over 4000 patients annually. Moreover, this approach would also help reduce healthcare costs associated with desensitization protocols and immunosuppressive treatment for incompatible transplants. In light of these findings, we propose a framework for a national kidney paired donation system that prioritizes patients based on their level of incompatibility and their waiting time, with the aim of maximizing the number of compatible transplants and minimizing healthcare costs. This framework also includes guidelines for managing waiting lists, coordinating exchanges between pairs, and allocating spots in the pool of potential donors and recipients. This research investigates how word embeddings are influenced by the composition of terms in various text corpora. In Natural Language Processing, word embeddings are widely applied, yet little is known about the underlying principles that govern these representations. We analyze the effects of five distinct term distribution characteristics - frequency, part-of-speech, co-occurrence, semantic similarity, and narrative structure - on the embeddings generated using two popular techniques, Word2Vec and GloVe. Our findings reveal that these models capture common aspects of term distributions but also reflect idiosyncrasies in specific corpora, such as the reliance on just a few influential texts to determine the embeddings of quoted passages. We further demonstrate that these hidden patterns in the embeddings enable them to make predictions about unseen text components, thereby enhancing their accuracy. Our research provides insights into the internal workings of word embeddings and suggests that their performance is partly a result of simply emulating the statistical properties of training data. To facilitate further research, we have made the code and our corpora publicly available. Our work has implications for the use of word embeddings in applications like sentiment analysis and text classification, and highlights the potential risks of overreliance on features that are essentially a copy of the input data. Next, we analyze specific two-agent games and identify patterns that allow us to reach CCE through rationalizable learning. We propose a Bayesian approach that fits PDFs using a mixture model, thereby enabling the incorporation of multiple, potentially incompatible datasets. The method focuses on a general set of PDF fitting constraints, with the aim of producing a set of optimal constraints that can be used to fit specific PDF fitting targets. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach using simulated deep learning output and PDF data. Furthermore, we apply this method to a real-world scenario involving LHC jet production data. The resulting PDF fits are compared to alternative methods, revealing that our approach yields consistent results with a marginal improvement in $\chi^2$ values. The associated code is available online, enabling users to integrate diverse datasets into PDF fitting procedures. The approach we present can be adapted for use in future PDF fitting initiatives, given the anticipated growth in machine learning-based hadron collider data. The underlying method is theoretically sound and its applicability is expected to extend beyond current LHC limitations to future high-energy colliders. The PDF fits generated using this approach are openly accessible within the HEPfit package, alongside other PDF sets. Selecting the most relevant past experiences to reuse in reinforcement learning
training is crucial, as using random memories can slow down convergence.
Traditional experience replay uses all past transitions equally, which is
inefficient due to the age of old experiences. Inspired by the concept of
time-differentiated value functions, we introduce a novel age-based value
extraction method to enhance the efficiency of experience replay. In this
approach, older experiences contribute less to policy updates, with contributions
proportional to their ages. We prove that the proposed algorithm converges to
an optimal policy under general conditions and provide sample-efficient learning
bounds. Furthermore, we demonstrate its effectiveness through policy gradient
methods in both discrete and continuous action spaces. Our results show that
older experiences can be ignored without loss of generality, as evidenced by
the tight sample complexity bounds in both offline and online settings. Our
approach can be viewed as a general framework for age-based experience replay,
with applications to various prioritization schemes, including uniform and
exponential weighting. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhongyuyu1998/
age_replay. 

The code is written in PyTorch and PyTorch Lightning, with the experience
replay module integrated into standard policy gradient training loops. Our
experiments utilize the standard experience replay data management provided
with PyTorch.

schemes, including uniform and exponential weighting, as shown in our
additional experiment results. Our approach can be applied to both discrete and
continuous action spaces, as well as offline and online learning settings.

estimation using policy gradient methods. Our age-based experience replay

implementations, with minimal modifications required to the underlying code.

including weighted and adaptive schemes. Our code includes detailed documentation

Our primary goal in creating the MultiTalk Dataset is to enhance the capabilities of conversational dialogue systems by enabling them to engage in discussions across diverse and unrelated topics. This dataset stands out from existing conversational datasets that focus on in-depth discussions about a single topic. With 5000 minutes of high-quality spoken data, the MultiTalk Dataset is the largest of its kind to date, featuring four participants who engage in 20-minute conversations about four randomly assigned topics. Notably, the structure of these conversations is designed to facilitate exploration of new tasks, such as identifying whether two pieces of text discuss the same topic, determining the relevance of a piece of text to a given topic, and categorizing conversations into distinct clusters based on their content. When put to use in evaluating a state-of-the-art conversational system, Reformer-based on the ConvS2S architecture, it shows significant improvement, with a gain of 6% in the emporer score. The code and dataset are available at https://github.com/google-research/MultiTalkDataset.

Specifically, they considered the relationship between these pairings and chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution. This paper develops Gaussian free field laws for various domains that result from Riemann surface techniques and connects them to the Dyson model and the stochastic process known as the looptiling, driven by a Brownian motion. Furthermore, we establish that these laws are distinct from the ones derived from the Dyson model and the stochastic process known as the looptiling, driven by the radial SLE$_6$ process. The results also include Gaussian free field laws for the domains created by the intersection of an SLE$_\kappa$ curve driven by a $\kappa$-dynamical Brownian motion and its complement, for $\kappa$ within the phase transition interval [4,8]. These laws are invariant under the Markov property of the underlying dynamics. This research investigates the impact of heat release variations in turbulent flames and their effect on acoustic fluctuations within a combustion chamber. A key aspect of this study is the development of an efficient numerical method to simulate flame-acoustic interactions over extended periods. By accounting for the random nature of heat release in the model, the study reveals the presence of distinct frequency ranges of flame noise that are influenced by different turbulence characteristics. Specifically, the study finds that the amplitude of the highest frequency noise is determined by the mean flame area, while the middle frequency range is affected by the mean heat release and flame speed, and the lowest frequency range is influenced by the chamber size and the mean flow velocity. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that flame noise models can be improved by incorporating the effects of heat release fluctuations, and it highlights the importance of accurately modeling these fluctuations to minimize errors in predictions of noise amplitudes. Additionally, the study reveals that the application of a linear model to predict flame noise in a combustion chamber of a real engine is feasible and yields reliable predictions of noise amplitudes across a wide range of engine speeds. However, it also shows that the model overestimates the noise in lower frequency ranges, indicating that nonlinear effects are more pronounced in these frequency ranges. Notably, the study demonstrates that the mean heat release per cycle can be estimated from flame noise measurements, and it presents a nonlinear model that accounts for the effects of mean heat release on flame noise in a real engine. This model exhibits a higher accuracy in predicting noise amplitudes than a linear model, particularly in frequency ranges dominated by combustion chamber dynamics. It also highlights the importance of accurately modeling the mean heat release per cycle to minimize errors in predictions of noise amplitudes. This research contributes to the development of more realistic models of flame noise and its interaction with combustion chamber acoustics, and it provides a framework for the application of these models in the design and optimization of combustion systems. This is demonstrated through the simulation of a combustion system with a membrane and the optimization of this system to minimize noise levels. This study is relevant to the development of more efficient and quieter combustion systems equipped with membranes, and it highlights the potential benefits of using membrane combustion systems. Nonlocal gravity theory is a classical generalization of Einstein's gravity theory. Based on an analogy with nonlocal electrodynamics, this new model involves a history-dependent relation between stress-energy tensors. Nonlocal gravity effects can be quantified through a memory function, and we derive this function using the nonlocal action equation. A key aspect of nonlocal gravity is that it gives rise to interactions between different gravitational fields and their time-evolution, and we explore the implications of this for scalar, vector, and tensor mass profiles in a static and spherically symmetric context. The resulting mass profiles are determined numerically and the nonlocal effects are found to alter the point-massature radius by $1.5$ units of the nonlocal timescale, and the nonlocal gravity can also give rise to the formation of black holes from scalar field condensation. The nonlocal gravity theory also leads to a non-zero nonlocal mass for linearized gravitational waves in an otherwise vacuum spacetime. The nonlocal mass scale can be constrained using the gravitational wave data from GW170817, yielding an upper bound of $7.5 \times 10^{-10}$ seconds$^{-1}$, or $1.5 \times 10^{-9}$ seconds$^{-1}$ if we consider the 95\% confidence level for the mass multipole. The nonlocal gravity theory can be tested further using the merger and ringdown signals from binary black hole mergers detected in gravitational wave data. The nonlocal gravity theory also predicts the existence of a minimum nonlocal length scale, below which the theory becomes unstable and the nonlocal memory function becomes negative, although this scale can be below the Planck length. The nonlocal gravity theory can be experimentally tested using laboratory experiments involving gravitational waves in finite settings. The nonlocal gravity theory also predicts the existence of nonlocal effects in the orbital angular momentum of binary systems, which could be detectable using high-precision astrometry. This tool leverages publicly accessible data and incorporates the effects of genetic variations on gene expression and chromatin structure. By combining multiple sources of information, VCT can pinpoint the most influential regions within genes linked to specific traits, and we've applied it to analyze 13 traits with known genetic underpinnings, revealing that the majority of associated SNPs coincide with accessible chromatin segments near their corresponding genes. Furthermore, by integrating VCT with gene expression data, it highlights the critical role of transcription factor binding sites and the local environment on gene function and expression. Our findings also suggest that certain SNPs linked to traits are often situated within transcription factor binding sites or in areas of chromatin that influence gene expression in their surrounding regions. Our research and tool are available for use by the scientific community at large.

Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center using the MegaCam at the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope reveal a significant population of quiescent low mass X-ray binaries that contain neutron stars. A statistical analysis of 24 established sources with measured luminosities indicates that the recurrence times for most of these sources are too short to be explained by typical neutron star accretion scenarios, suggesting that substantial amounts of mass must have been transferred to the stars in the past. Furthermore, a correlation exists between the recurrence times and the values of specific spectral features in their optical spectra, which can be linked to the masses of their binary companions. This finding is consistent with earlier observations of a similar binary system, RY Scuti, and may be indicative of a broader phenomenon observed in many binary systems that contain a massive donor star that has undergone significant mass loss through a strong wind. This mass loss could be a result of the operation of a symbiotic giant wind, fueled by the energy released from the binary's interaction, and may also contribute to the formation of the surrounding circumstellar medium within the Milky Way's center. This medium is thought to be a significant source of high-energy particles that power the extreme ultraviolet radiation observed in the Milky Way's center. This hypothesis is supported by numerical modeling of the evolution of binary systems that contain a massive donor star and a neutron star, and can also explain the observed distributions of recurrence times and the values of specific spectral features in their optical spectra. This hypothesis can be tested by means of future high-energy particle and magnetic field measurements within the Milky Way's center. This study also highlights the importance of optical spectroscopy in the understanding of the populations of low mass X-ray binaries within the Milky Way's center, and in the search for variations in the values of specific spectral features in their optical spectra that could be linked to changes in the mass loss from these systems and the surrounding circumstellar medium within the Milky Way's center. This study also emphasizes the need for further high-energy particle and magnetic field measurements within the Milky Way's center, and the potential of the next generation of MegaCam at the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope for the discovery of new variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center. This study also provides a detailed analysis of the optical spectroscopy of 24 established low mass X-ray binaries within the Milky Way's center, and a catalog of their basic parameters. This study also presents a method for estimating the masses of the secondary stars in binary systems that contain a neutron star,

THz radiation enables the precise and controlled manipulation of electrons' motion and the vibration of atoms and molecules. In a study involving a potassium-based superconducting material, YBCO, researchers utilized a powerful THz source to synchronize the vibration of oxygen atoms with the circular motion of electrons at the Fermi level, leading to a novel type of spin-orbit interaction. By applying this technique, the authors achieved a level of control over the distribution of charge carriers, allowing them to create areas with high carrier density and localized areas with carrier-free gaps at the Fermi level. This breakthrough offers a new method for engineering the properties of materials and potentially reveals a mechanism for high-temperature superconductivity. Furthermore, the unique ability to modulate the distribution of charge carriers through THz radiation may provide a means for optimizing the performance of YBCO for various applications. This discovery also opens up possibilities for exploring the interplay between spin-orbit interaction, carrier distribution, and the material's electromagnetic response. As a result, the study's findings can be applied to a wide range of materials exhibiting spin-orbit coupling, such as other cuprates and transition metal dichalcogenides. Ultimately, this research demonstrates that the controlled manipulation of carrier distribution and the vibration of atoms through THz radiation can significantly impact the field of materials science and condensed matter physics. This achievement can be utilized to create novel materials and phenomena resulting from the interaction between spin-orbit coupling, carrier distribution, and the electromagnetic field, leading to potential breakthroughs in fields like materials engineering, optics, and quantum physics. This study was conducted by combining advanced spectroscopies, including angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, X-ray absorption spectroscopy, and terahertz time-domain spectroscopy, and was supported by theoretical models based on first-principles simulations. This research was carried out by an international team of scientists from institutions located in Japan, Germany, and the United States. This breakthrough was made possible by the development of a powerful THz source with an extremely high level of coherence, achieved through the use of a photoelectric converter and a photoacoustic detector in a specially designed setup. engaging responses in extended conversations is a significant challenge. To tackle
this issue, we develop a comprehensive framework that assesses response diversity
using three key metrics. Firstly, it evaluates the semantic variety of individual
responses through a Natural Language Inference task. To enhance semantic diversity,
we introduce a Natural Language Inference dataset with multiple suitable gold
labels for each NLI instance, which we call NLI Multiple Choice. With 20,000
instances, NLI MC surpasses existing NLI benchmarks in both semantic similarity
and relatedness. Secondly, we employ a set-based semantic similarity measure to
quantify the semantic variety of single responses. Lastly, we design a diverse
response generator based on a rich knowledge base and employ set-based semantic
similarity to guide the selection of diverse responses during knowledge graph
traversal. Through extensive experiments, our framework and associated datasets
demonstrate substantial improvements in response diversity, achieving near-human
performance. To further advance in response diversity, we encourage the community
to explore more sophisticated models and consider the economic cost of increased

As expected, rotation caused these stars to become oblate, but it also led to the formation of hot, dense cores at their centers. When the accretion rate exceeded a certain limit, these cores became so hot that they ignited hydrogen in their cores, but this often resulted in the stars losing this core and only burning hydrogen on their surfaces, rather than sustainably burning hydrogen. As a result, a stable hydrogen-burning phase became less likely as rotation increased. Additionally, when the stars spun fast enough, their cores became too hot to cool radiatively, leading to their collapse into a white dwarf or neutron star. Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intensive, yet may not always guarantee satisfactory results due to the inherently complex and time-consuming nature of certain optimization problems associated with it. In contrast, a faster approach is proposed that splits the graph into distinct components, breaks down each into individual trees or required structures, and then reassembles the original graph from these simplified components, thereby significantly shortening processing time while producing more acceptable edge crossings. Experimental data indicates that this method yields lower edge crossings and a more compact layout within a shorter processing time compared to existing techniques. In cases where exact results are desired, this method can be used as a starting point for further optimization. In addition to its efficiency, this approach also produces visually appealing straight edge drawings, especially in instances where tree structures are prevalent. Experimental evaluations were conducted using randomly generated graphs as well as real-world data, consisting of Wikipedia co-authorship graphs and citation networks from arXiv and CiteSeerX. System implementation details and sample visualizations are available at https://crossreducer.org/. This method has been published in the Proceedings of the 2023 IEEE Pacific Visualization Conference as well as the IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics journal. A related issue of ordering nodes along a single line to minimize edge crossings is also addressed in this research, and its solution is presented as a part of the overall problem-solving strategy. In this particular problem variant, all edge crossings are eliminated at the cost of varying node orderings, and the associated algorithm is shown to be fast and accurate in finding optimal solutions, in addition to being capable of handling large-scale inputs. In contrast, existing algorithms for solving this variant problem have computationally intensive processing requirements. In this research, an example application is demonstrated where node orderings obtained from this variant problem are utilized to create effective and aesthetically pleasing treemaps. Experimental data confirms that this approach yields lower edge crossings and a more compact layout compared to traditional treemaps. This paper presents a novel walking mechanism that incorporates thrusters into a bipedal robot's design. By positioning thrusters at the lower end of the legs, we generate a pressurized air chamber that changes volume in sync with the gait cycle, enabling the robot to walk using the resulting pneumatic impedance. The proposed method eliminates the need for actuators in the joints, thereby reducing the system's complexity and allowing for quieter and more efficient locomotion. Moreover, the thrusters can be powered by a single motor, making it an energy-efficient solution. Theoretical and simulation-based analyses are conducted to evaluate the proposed approach, and we also provide experimental results from a prototype to demonstrate the feasibility of this idea. The findings from these studies can be applied to the design of similar robots utilizing pneumatic impedance in their walking mechanism. The proposed method's advantages make it suitable for use in quiet, efficient, and complex robot applications. Recent research has demonstrated the effectiveness of side-channel attacks leveraging microarchitectural flaws in neural networks, and such attacks can be enhanced by exploiting simultaneous multithreading architectures. However, current SMT side-channel attack methods primarily target performance-enhancing techniques and overlook various other microarchitectural features that can be exploited for side-channel attacks. In this paper, a novel performance degradation technique called Neural Network Thread Latency Exploitation (NITLE) is introduced, which leverages the variability of thread latency in SMT architectures to enhance the accuracy of machine learning models for side-channel attacks. To achieve this, a unique dataset consisting of 2000 distinct thread latency samples was collected on a real-world Intel Xeon Gold 5118 processor, and a deep learning model was trained and validated using this data. Our results show that using NITLE, side-channel attack accuracy can be improved by approximately 10% when targeting a single thread, and approximately 15% when targeting multiple threads. Furthermore, NITLE was found to be a complementary technique to other side-channel attacks, as demonstrated in our experiments. In summary, this paper presents a pioneering attempt to explore the use of thread latency in SMT architectures for side-channel attacks, and its effectiveness in enhancing such attacks. A localized alteration in knot diagrams can change a knot into its "untangled" form, and this process is known as an unknotting operation. Various methods for accomplishing an unknotting operation have been identified and categorized into distinct types. This study delves into the examination of a specific unknotting operation, referred to as the "twist unlinking operation," and seeks to establish a connection between this operation and another well-known phenomenon called the "twist reduction property." A step-by-step, graphical representation of how the twist unlinking operation applies the twist reduction property to localized areas of a knot is demonstrated. Furthermore, this study also explores and explains how the twist unlinking operation can be used to graphically represent the process of removing twists from a knot, and it is shown that this operation can be used to break down any knot into its most basic components, known as "stick" knots. A computational tool has been developed to automate the twist unlinking operation for the purpose of identifying stick knots within a given database of knots. This tool was utilized in a search of all knots with up to 10 twists, resulting in the discovery of 242 distinct stick knots, as well as 19 previously unknown knots. One of these newly discovered knots has a twist count that is the lowest among all known knots with a specific length, and it is hypothesized that this record will likely be broken as more knots are searched. The method presented in this study can be applied to larger databases of knots, and it is anticipated that it will be valuable for future research aimed at better understanding the characteristics of knots. Kernel methods have proven highly effective in various machine learning applications, yet their scalability to large datasets is severely limited due to the computationally expensive nature of pairwise evaluations. In response, Random Fourier Features were proposed to approximate kernel functions using random transformations, thereby enabling the use of kernel methods on larger data sets. While this method has been successful in various contexts, it has been found to be particularly ineffective for translating data, particularly in the domain of natural language, where it has been shown to yield representations that are highly unstable and fail to capture meaningful semantic relationships. This study introduces an alternative method of approximating kernel functions through the use of all-but-one cosine similarity, which has been found to produce more stable and semantically meaningful representations. Furthermore, this study demonstrates the method's effectiveness in several machine learning tasks, including translation, and finds it to be particularly advantageous when combined with other successful transfer learning techniques. This method's efficacy is shown to be comparable to, and in some cases better than, the current state-of-the-art methods of kernel approximation. This research paper examines conformally flat hypersurfaces of n-dimensional space (n is 4 or higher) within a hypersphere of n+2 dimensions. We initially prove that a compact hypersurface with constant M\"obius scalar curvature can be classified into three distinct categories: (1) a hypersurface with constant curvature, (2) a hypersurface derived from a conformally flat hypersurface in n-dimensional space with constant scalar curvature, or (3) a hypersurface formed by combining multiple copies of a fundamental domain with constant scalar curvature. Next, we explore the topological properties of these hypersurfaces and determine that a compact hypersurface with constant M\"obius scalar curvature and specific values of mean and scalar curvatures can be classified into one of the two following configurations: (1) a hypersurface with constant curvature, or (2) a hypersurface composed of a specific number of copies of a fundamental domain with constant scalar curvature. Finally, we discuss the applications of these findings to simplify the proof of a key theorem regarding compact hypersurfaces. This theorem states that under certain curvature constraints, a hypersurface with positive volume must have a diameter less than or equal to $\sqrt{(n-1)(n+1)}$. This result helps to expand upon an earlier finding by Geroth and Rosenberg, as well as a subsequent improvement made by Geroth, and provides a preliminary step towards solving the Schurr Conjecture. This research extends and refines the findings of Geroth and Rosenberg, and also generalizes the hypersphere-based results from a previous paper by strengthening the dimensionality requirements from n=3 to n=4 or higher. In this context, we investigate the unknown quantity $\chi_c(N_t)$, which represents the smallest number of infected nodes needed to cause an avalanche of size $N_t$ in network $G$. To simplify the computation of this quantity, we propose an alternative measure called the effective size of a node, denoted as $s_i$, which indicates the minimum number of directly connected nodes required to cause an avalanche of size $N_t$ when starting from node $i$. Furthermore, we analyze the accuracy of this estimation and demonstrate its applicability to various network models. In addition, we introduce a network attack resilience metric called the maximum effective size, which represents the largest possible effective size when removing a specified number of malicious nodes. This quantity provides a threshold for distinguishing between network components with different attack outcomes. We also explore the connection between this quantity and the epidemic threshold in network dynamics. To facilitate the implementation of our algorithm, we develop a distributed framework that can be executed on a subset of nodes, and we discuss its scalability. This framework is particularly useful for large networks and can be employed in various real-world applications, including smart grids and transportation systems. In particular, we identify two major open problems related to the estimation of the effective size in networks: accurately determining the avalanche size and efficiently computing the minimum neighborhood size in each node. To address these challenges, we propose several future research directions. In addition, we outline the potential applications and implications of our work in the fields of network security, epidemiology, and complex systems dynamics. Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant difficulties due to frequent occlusions and the wide range of head poses present in images. To address this challenge, we develop a novel 3D face alignment and reconstruction framework that effectively handles these issues. Our approach begins with a two-dimensional face alignment network that identifies corresponding two-dimensional face points across various head poses and occluded instances. We then employ a 3D face reconstruction network to project a single, unified 3D face model onto the aligned two-dimensional points, producing a diverse set of pose- and occlusion-specific 3D face models as output. Unlike conventional methods that rely on explicit pose and occlusion estimation, our approach avoids these difficulties by directly projecting the 3D face models onto the aligned two-dimensional points. We further introduce a pose- and occlusion-aware loss function to guide the network in generating realistic 3D face models across varying head poses and occlusions. Our framework achieves state-of-the-art performance on the AFLW2000-3D and Florence datasets in face alignment and reconstruction tasks. Additionally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on challenging real-world datasets by applying our network to synthetic data, resulting in a network that can reconstruct faces in real-world images with diverse head poses and occlusions. Our code is available at: https://github.com/zhengyangyao/3D-Face-Reconstruction-Variety.

Researchers defined the "deepest level" of a marked ordered tree as the highest level containing at least one marked node.
They proved that the expected number of deepest nodes in marked ordered trees of $n$ nodes is $\frac{3}{2}$ when there are two marked nodes and $\left(1+\frac{1}{k}\right)^k$ when there are $k$ marked nodes.
Additionally, as the number of nodes increases, the expected number of deepest nodes in marked ordered trees with a fixed number of marked nodes converges to the root marked at level $\frac{n}{k}$.
Finally, determining the number of deepest nodes is shown to be equivalent to finding the highest level with at least one marked node in a uniform random marked ordered tree of a given size, and an explicit formula is given for the probability that a given level contains at least one marked node. 
This level-generating function generalizes the derivative of the exponential function, known as the Eulerian generating function. 
It can also represent the distribution of the number of nodes at a given level in uniform random ordered trees of a given size. 
Finally, the average distance from a marked node to the root in uniform random marked ordered trees of a given size is calculated as $\frac{2n+1}{k+2}$ when there are $k$ marked nodes. 
This result can be interpreted as showing that the distance from a marked node to the root in uniform random marked ordered trees of a given size follows a negative binomial distribution with parameters $k+2$ and $\frac{1}{2}$.

Our investigation focused on a HgTe quantum well with a thickness of 3.46 nm and the presence of a 6 nm thick CdHgTe barrier on one side, and a 20 nm thick CdTe barrier on the other. By applying a magnetic field, we observed a transition from a two-dimensional electron gas to a two-dimensional hole gas within the middle region of the well. As the field increased, we found a peak in the Hall resistance at 4.5 T, corresponding to a filling factor of one, and a significant increase in the Hall resistance at 6.5 T. Our findings are consistent with the formation of helical edge states within the middle region of the well, coupled with the transition from the two-dimensional hole gas. Our data also show resistance oscillations associated with the formation of Landau levels in the middle region of the well. By comparing our results with theoretical models, we found that the middle region of the well has a moderate disorder, and that the well's symmetry is broken, leading to the formation of helical edge states throughout the entire range of filling factors. Notably, the resistance peaks at the filling factor of one are higher than those observed in smaller wells, indicating that the middle region of the well exhibits unique behavior. Our study highlights the unique properties of this particular well and the need for further investigation into the formation of helical edge states. Our findings are also consistent with theoretical predictions, showing that the middle region of the well behaves as a separate entity with its own set of properties. Our data are supported by numerical simulations of the Landau level fan diagram, and simulations of the resistance and magnetization curves. Our study opens up new avenues for further investigation into the unique properties of this particular well and the middle region of quantum wells under a magnetic field. Our research also highlights the potential applications of this phenomenon in the development of advanced spintronics devices. In this work, we introduce a novel meta-learning framework centered on ODE neural networks, which acquires a generalized optimization procedure rather than a gradient descent rule. We demonstrate that this model excels over the conventional approach by avoiding the difficulties associated with estimating the number of training iterations. The success of this method is shown to be versatile, with applications to both meta-optimization problems and machine learning tasks. Specifically, it yields a data-efficient solution for classifying handwritten digits and another that applies to the parametrization of continuous-time dynamics. In both instances, we establish the convergence of the proposed algorithm to a meaningful target, with corresponding theoretical guarantees for the accuracy of learned models. Our code is publicly accessible at: https://github.com/zheng557/odes-for-meta-learning. 

To begin, we outline a general optimization problem where the target function depends on an arbitrary input, along with an input-output relationship represented by an ordinary differential equation. We then extract this target function as the initial condition of an ordinary differential equation, which we term an "inference system." In essence, this strategy treats the target function as an unknown starting condition of an ordinary differential equation, whose underlying dynamics corresponds to the ODE network. We establish that when the underlying dynamics is identifiable, we can recover the target function through a meta-learning process that involves solving a optimization problem, with solutions provided by our proposed algorithm. Ultimately, this algorithm enables us to infer the target function from a set of training examples, with performance guarantees that reflect the uniqueness of the underlying dynamics. 

Our research is underpinned by several key concepts, including the idea of a "dynamical dictionary," which we define as a set of distinct ordinary differential equations whose solutions can be combined to produce a wide variety of target functions. We establish that a "dynamical dictionary" is equivalent to a universal approximator similar to neural networks, with corresponding requirements for its size and complexity. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between the regularity of the underlying dynamics, the smoothness of the target function, and the performance of our meta-learning algorithm. Our results also reveal that our algorithm can succeed even when the underlying dynamics is non-identifiable, under the condition that the set of starting conditions is compact and the underlying dynamics is dynamically regular. In addition, we demonstrate that our algorithm can be viewed as a form of regularization that enforces the smoothness of the target function, with associated performance guarantees.

This research introduces the $n$th toroidal colored Jones polynomial, labeled as $J_n^T$, which extends the colored Jones polynomial, and demonstrates that $J_n^T$ shares the same nuances as the original colored Jones polynomial, specifically its relationship with the Casson invariant and volume conjecture. Notably, $J_n^T$ is distinguished from the Kauffman bracket skein relation, and we propose an alternative relation to generate $J_n^T$. Additionally, $J_n^T$ can be realized through a link's biperiodic volume, and we establish an inductive formula to compute $J_n^T$ for split links. Furthermore, $J_n^T$ satisfies the same weighted arithmetic-geometric mean (WAGM) equation as the original colored Jones polynomial. This extends the WAGM equation to a toroidal setting, providing a framework for studying the quantum invariants of links within a $3$-manifold. This research also introduces the $n$th toroidal colored Jones polynomial's coefficients, denoted as $\{K_n^T(\mu)\}_{\mu \in P_n}$, and shows that these coefficients correspond to the weighted dimensions of a toroidal topological quantum field theory, specifically the $n$th Turaev-Le, and Bar-Natan-Le TQFT. This connection enables the computation of $K_n^T(\mu)$ for any link $L$ within a $3$-manifold $M$, by employing the properties of the TQFT. This research also proposes an extension of the volume conjecture for the colored Jones polynomial, which posits that the coefficients of the $n$th toroidal colored Jones polynomial are equal to the weighted dimensions of the Turaev-Le, and Bar-Natan-Le TQFT. This is supported by numerical data obtained from the volume of a toroidal knot, specifically the figure-eight knot. This research provides a framework for studying the quantum invariants of links within a $3$-manifold, and offers insights into the volume conjecture, which remains an open problem. To account for this ambiguity, we propose a probabilistic framework that assigns weighted senses for a given word in a particular context. This model is then utilized to calculate the precision, recall, and F-score, taking into consideration the possibility of multiple sense interpretations. This paper introduces a novel end-to-end cross-domain text-to-SQL model, which employs a dual-representation learning approach to tackle crucial components in SQL generation: schema selection and attribute extraction. Our proposed framework, called DRSNet, manipulates a unified representation space to distinguish between two tasks, leveraging a dual-task contrastive learning method to enhance performance. DRSNet achieves state-of-the-art results on CrossDomainSQL, a benchmark for cross-domain text-to-SQL tasks, and also excels in two individual domains, SynthDB and RestauDB. Our model's effectiveness is attributed to its ability to balance schema selection and attribute extraction through learned weights, and we provide insights into these findings through rigorous ablation studies. Furthermore, our work provides a theoretical analysis of the dual-representation learning method, and presents several practical guidelines for building high-performance text-to-SQL models. Our code and model are available at https://github.com/zhanglei1993/DRSNet.

This paper explores the application of differential privacy to graph-based data, which has an intricate structure that must be considered when developing private algorithms. A key challenge in this context arises from the adjacency matrix representation of graphs, as small changes to the adjacency matrix can result in significant alterations to the neighborhood relationships and, consequently, the output of many graph-based algorithms. Compared to previous research, this work has effectively mapped the lowest part of the nuclear spectrum in 64Ni, and its findings challenge current shell-model theories. According to our analysis, 64Ni's low-spin states are analogous to 62Ni's states but are shifted upwards by about 500 keV, and our data also show that 64Ni's collective 2+1 state is missing, with the first missing state appearing at 3.43 MeV in a 64Ni reaction involving 58Ni, and at 3.37 MeV in a 64Ni reaction involving 60Ni. Our research suggests that 64Ni's low-spin state energy patterns are influenced by both nuclear reactions and the composition of its parent nuclei. When subjected to high stresses, the vast majority of dense mixtures undergo a sudden and extreme thickening, characterized by a shift from forcefully pushed particles to strongly attractive particles. Despite the critical importance of this transition in understanding various geological and engineering phenomena, the underlying mechanisms driving this thickening transition remain poorly understood. This study investigates the thickening transition of polyethyleneamino functionalized glass spheres in glycerol, utilizing ultrafast imaging to capture the rapid deformation and subsequent recovery of the suspension. By analyzing the suspension's viscoelastic behavior and comparing it to theoretical models, we found that the transition is explained by the deformation of particles interacting through electrostatic forces, rather than rigid interactions. Furthermore, we found that the suspension's behavior during the transition can be accurately described by a model that accounts for the compression of particles and the formation of bonds between particles, and this model successfully predicts the effects of shear stress and particle size on the suspension's properties. Notably, we found that the bond lifetime under high shear stress conditions is significantly shorter than previously reported, and this finding has important implications for the understanding of various geological and engineering phenomena, including the behavior of clay in shear stress conditions, and the jamming of particles in venturi tubes. This study provides a fundamental understanding of the mechanisms driving the thickening transition of dense suspensions under high shear stress, and it has important implications for the development of constitutive models that describe the behavior of these systems. This study also highlights the importance of accurately characterizing particle interactions and the effects of surface chemistry on particle interactions, and it emphasizes the critical role of surface chemistry in controlling the behavior of particles in various applications. Web search engines tailor results to individual users based on their past behaviour, which can be both beneficial and detrimental. While it makes searches more efficient, it may cause users to overlook vital details, particularly in critical situations like medical emergencies. To address this concern, we propose an alternative search approach, WebNomad, which conducts searches anonymously and aggregates information from multiple results to counter the limitations of personalisation. By examining user interactions and adapting its strategy, WebNomad identifies potentially relevant data and combines the most crucial information into a concise summary. We tested WebNomad in two real-world applications: finding medical information for rare diseases and gathering information about products to buy on Amazon. In both cases, WebNomad located substantially more relevant data than a typical search engine, and its summary contained a large portion of the available information - potentially 75% could be missed due to search personalisation.

Continuous Acquisition Turbo Partial-Flip (CAT-PF) is a novel MRI acquisition approach that addresses respiratory motion's impact on image quality. This method continuously collects raw data during free-breathing scans and uses a turbo partial-flip technique to enhance resolution. CAT-PF compensates for the decrease in signal caused by partial flip angles and allows for the construction of high-resolution images from low-resolution intermediates. This method's performance was evaluated in cat brain and abdominal scans in rats, and it was found to effectively reduce motion-induced artifacts while meeting safety guidelines for MRI signal levels. CAT-PF's efficacy in creating high-resolution images from under-sampled and irregular data makes it suitable for various applications, including real-time MRI and accelerated whole-body scans. A key aspect of CAT-PF is its ability to maintain compatibility with advanced reconstruction techniques like compressed sensing. Experimental results indicate that CAT-PF can achieve comparable or better image quality compared to traditional techniques, with reduced scan duration and improved patient comfort. A 4D extension of CAT-PF has been proposed to accommodate dynamic data acquisition. This approach has been applied to dynamic abdominal imaging in rats and demonstrated CAT-PF's potential for tracking rapid physiological changes over time. Despite its advantages, CAT-PF faces technical challenges related to its long scan duration, specifically in high-field MRI systems. Nonetheless, its potential for improving MRI image quality makes it an area worthy of further investigation.
