In contrast, we've developed an efficient algorithm for calculating paired-permutation test results, significantly reducing computation time. Our approach takes the form of a dynamic programming problem, which we've solved using a novel linearization. This linearization enables us to leverage highly optimized existing solutions, resulting in a substantial decrease in computation time for the paired-permutation test. In particular, our method allows us to calculate paired-permutation test results at least 50 times faster than existing Monte Carlo methods. We've made our code publicly available to facilitate wider adoption and improvement of this method. In addition, we've conducted a series of experiments to validate our approach and provide guidelines for optimizing computation time. Notably, our results indicate that the paired-permutation test often yields very small p-values, which can be seen as indicating that many existing NLP evaluation metrics are not sufficiently sensitive to detect meaningful differences in performance. To illustrate this, we've conducted a series of controlled experiments involving both automatic evaluation metrics and human judgments. These experiments have shown that while the paired-permutation test often finds statistically significant differences between models based on automatic evaluation metrics, similar differences are not found when human judgments are used. This observation has significant implications for the NLP community, suggesting that the paired-permutation test can serve as a valuable tool for highlighting the limitations of current evaluation methods and encouraging the development of more effective ones. In particular, our results indicate that the paired-permutation test can be used to conduct a form of cross-validation that helps evaluate the generalizability of NLP models. This evaluation of generalizability, in turn, can be used to assess the impact of various factors such as the size of training data, the use of specific techniques like dropout, and the choice of evaluation metrics. Our research also sheds light on the characteristics of models that exhibit low variance in performance, which can be used to identify key differences between them. Finally, our results demonstrate that the paired-permutation test can be used to compare the performance of NLP models across multiple tasks, which we believe can be a valuable contribution to the development of more effective comparison methods. A comprehensive dataset of freight rates, shipping quantities, new ship prices, used ship prices, and scrapped ship prices has been assembled from 1966 to 2009 for six major shipping routes. This unique compilation enables researchers to examine historical trends and relationships within the shipping industry. Former hypotheses about the industry's behavior are challenged using graphical visualizations and time-series analysis. It is shown that the industry's past patterns of stability were actually characterized by volatility and that key events such as the 1997-1999 container crisis and the 1973 oil price shock had more far-reaching impacts than previously thought. A critical review of the proposed solutions to the container crisis is also presented. It is argued that the industry's problems are better explained by its own internal dynamics than by external factors. Further analysis of the data reveals that the relationships within the industry are complex and have altered over time. It is also found that the industry's behavior can be described as self-organizing and that the structure of its markets has shifted in response to changes in the industry. It is concluded that shipping markets cannot be accurately modeled using traditional economic theories and that more complex approaches are required. It is also suggested that the industry's behavior could be better understood by applying the principles of chaos theory. It is further proposed that the development of the container crisis was facilitated by a combination of factors including a significant increase in shipping quantities, a decline in new ship prices, and an unexpected surge in demand for ship scrapping. It is estimated that the container crisis resulted in the destruction of over 100 million tons of shipping capacity at a cost of $10 billion. It is also found that the industry's capacity for self-correction is limited and that it is prone to sudden and extreme shifts in behavior. It is suggested that this characteristic of the industry makes it particularly vulnerable to external shocks. It is also proposed that the application of chaos theory could provide a useful framework for understanding the risks associated with shipping investments. It is further suggested that a better understanding of the industry's behavior could be achieved by conducting further research into the relationships between shipping quantities, prices, and capacities using complex dynamic models. It is also proposed that the development of more accurate forecasting tools for shipping prices and quantities could be achieved by conducting further research into the use of time-series analysis and machine learning algorithms. It is also suggested that the industry's behavior could be improved by conducting further research into the design of more effective regulatory policies using complex dynamic models. We define loom spaces as a more general framework incorporating leaf spaces for pseudo-Anosov flows and link spaces for veering triangulations. Building on Giannis's findings, we prove that veering triangulations associated with a loom space's monodromy determine that loom space uniquely, and that there exists an explicit construction from the veering triangulation to the loom space. Furthermore, this construction allows for an increase in the genus, resulting in the generalization of a statement by Purcivral. Additionally, veering triangulations can be recovered from a loom space's monodromy, providing a foundation for defining veering triangulations from a loom space's monodromy in increased genus settings. Lastly, we explore the relationship between loom spaces and veering triangulations near ramification points. This research was inspired by Bonino's work on the veering regulator and its connection to loom spaces. As a result, we can define the veering regulator for any loom space. Notably, this expands upon Bonino's initial findings, allowing for an explicit computation of the veering regulator for any given loom space. This computation reveals that the veering regulator's volume is equivalent to the loom space's measure, solidifying the connection between these two concepts. This research was also motivated by a desire to expand upon the ideas presented in Bonino's work with the aim of creating a more comprehensive understanding of the veering regulator's properties. This expanded understanding reveals that the veering regulator's volume is directly related to the loom space's measure. This relationship provides a tangible, measurable representation of the veering regulator's volume, thereby solidifying the connection between the veering regulator and loom spaces. This research was also inspired by the desire to generalize a statement found in Purcivral's work. This generalized statement allows for an increase in the genus of a loom space's associated veering triangulation. This generalized statement was achieved by developing a method for constructing veering triangulations from a loom space's monodromy in increased genus settings. This achievement provides a foundation for defining veering triangulations from a loom space's monodromry in these same increased genus settings. This research also explores the relationship between loom spaces and veering triangulations near ramification points. This investigation was motivated by a desire to expand upon the ideas presented in Bonino's work with the aim of creating a more comprehensive understanding of veering triangulations near these points.

The recent surge in financial news consumption on social media platforms, coupled with the growing accessibility of real-time stock market data, has created a significant opportunity to develop a stock prediction model grounded in sentiment analysis. This study combines a deep learning approach with a technical analysis module to create a highly accurate stock forecasting model. Initially, the Reuters corpus was utilized to train a Bi-directional Long Short-Term Memory network in identifying positive and negative sentiment within financial news headlines. The output was then fed into a technical analysis module, where indicators such as moving averages and relative strength index were integrated to enhance forecasting performance. This model was tested across multiple companies and time frames, yielding notable improvements over baseline models. Specifically, when applied to Apple Inc., the model demonstrated a 3.08% return on investment within a 7-day period, and a 5.56% return on investment within a 30-day period. This research shows that, with sufficient data, a deep learning approach can effectively capture the complex relationships between financial news sentiment and stock prices. Consequently, this model has the potential to be applied in real-world scenarios, provided that sufficient historical stock and news data is accessible. This study is particularly relevant to the Chinese stock market due to the widespread use of sentiment analysis in predicting stock prices among Chinese investors. This research also highlights the challenges associated with applying Western financial text corpora to the analysis of Chinese stock prices. This issue is further explored in the subsequent study presented in this paper. This research is part of a larger project that aims to develop a framework for constructing a Chinese text corpus tailored to the analysis of stock prices. This framework takes into account the linguistic characteristics of Chinese text, and it has been applied to create two such corpora, one for positive sentiment and one for negative sentiment. This research examines double Higgs boson production at future electron-positron colliders CLIC and ILC with TeV-scale energies within the framework of Effective Field Theories (EFTs), specifically the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT). We investigate both the dominant and negligible contributions to the process $e^+ e^-\rightarrow HH$ using the Weak Value Insertion (WVI) and Weak Value Insertion at the Double Higgs Vertex (WDVV) effective operators. Furthermore, we find that the WDVV operator's detection threshold is significantly higher, at approximately $10^{-4}$. The cylinder was oriented both perpendicular and parallel to its long axis as it moved, and we found that the drag it experienced differed significantly in the two orientations, a phenomenon we call anisotropy. This anisotropy varied greatly with the speed at which the cylinder was moved and its speed relative to the grains, but it consistently followed a particular pattern when slowed down to a crawl. Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on centrality, we discovered minimal variation in triangular flow centrality. However, once the influence of initial geometry was removed, we observed an increase in $v_3/\epsilon_3$ in proportion to transverse particle density, mirroring $v_2/\epsilon_2$'s behavior. Additionally, we found triangular and elliptical flow to exhibit analogous transverse momentum dependencies for identified particles. These findings suggest that triangular flow's centrality independence may be an indicator of quark gluon plasma's medium sensitivity to initial anisotropic charges. Moreover, our results indicate a similarity in physics driving both elliptical and triangular flow behavior.

Soft-tissue navigation is a non-rigid registration technique used to track and guide surgical procedures such as tumor resection and organ repair. Real-time data from intraoperative ultrasound is registered against preoperative MRI scans to create a 3D model of soft tissues. This challenge has sparked interest in developing and testing non-rigid registration methods for real-time applications. We present a testing framework for evaluating the performance of non-rigid registration algorithms in a realistic simulation environment. This framework incorporates a ground-truth reference for registration accuracy and assesses multiple performance metrics across various simulation scenarios. We demonstrate the framework's effectiveness by evaluating a widely used non-rigid registration method and identify areas for improving the simulation settings to better capture real-world registration variability. Our testing framework is designed to facilitate the development and testing of new non-rigid registration techniques, and we encourage researchers to leverage and contribute to this framework. We make the framework publicly available at https://github.com/ctang3/soft_tissue_registration_benchmark. Evaluations and benchmark data are accessible at https://results.osf.io/andingid/5yj9k/. Determining scene flow involves calculating the three-dimensional displacement information for points within an image by analyzing multiple frames. Motion vector estimation is a crucial component in various applications such as gesture analysis, vehicle navigation, and facial expression recognition. In recent years, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) have demonstrated superior performance in point-to-point displacement prediction by treating the problem as a binary classification task, albeit being computationally intensive. In contrast, a Convolutional Neural Descriptor (CND) is proposed to efficiently determine three-dimensional displacement at three-dimensional points within an image by analyzing a single frame. This Convolutional Neural Descriptor consists of two main components: a Residual Flow Network that generates preliminary displacement information and an Upsample Module that refines this information. In evaluating this method, a large Scene Flow Dataset is utilized, yielding a mean point-to-point Euclidean distance error of 7.04 mm and mean flow re-projection error of 11.38%. This Convolutional Neural Descriptor demonstrates its effectiveness in real-world scenarios by analyzing a Middlebury Dataset and a Stanford 7-Scenes Dataset. In addition, this model exhibits a mean flow re-projection error of 12.53% on a newly created Mini Scene Flow Dataset with 0.5 mm average point displacement. In comparison to state-of-the-art CNN-based models, this Convolutional Neural Descriptor achieves comparable performance at a significantly reduced computational cost. In particular, at a resolution of 640x480, its point-to-point Euclidean distance error is 7.04 mm and mean flow re-projection error is 11.38%. This Convolutional Neural Descriptor is a highly efficient and accurate scene flow estimation algorithm suitable for various applications, particularly those involving real-time analysis. In such cases, it can be used as a standalone model, while in non-real-time scenarios, it can be used in conjunction with other algorithms to fine-tune its results. In particular, it is demonstrated that by combining this model with a Convolutional Neural Network-based metric learning algorithm and a Convolutional Neural Network-based classification algorithm, it is possible to improve their performance in vehicle navigation and facial expression recognition, respectively. In particular, with the Convolutional Neural Descriptor, the mean classification accuracy on a FER2013 Dataset is increased from 65.45% to 83.45%. In recent years, AI networks that rely on artificial neurons have significantly outperformed competitors in various tasks and had a substantial impact on various fields. However, their extensive computational needs have hindered their real-world implementation. In contrast, biological neural networks inspired by the behavior of actual neurons have been shown to be highly energy-efficient. A specific type, known as Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs), has demonstrated superior performance and low power consumption. Despite these benefits, training SNNs has been a challenging and time-consuming process due to the limited availability of efficient algorithms. In this research, a novel method for training SNNs was developed by integrating a spiking reservoir with a genetic algorithm. The reservoir's output was used as input for a fitness evaluation, and the underlying parameters were modified using a genetic algorithm. As a result, the network was capable of solving complex problems with a high degree of accuracy and required minimal parameters. In addition, the proposed framework was put to use in two real-world applications: a biometric authentication system and an air quality prediction system. In both instances, the network's performance was compared to conventional methods, and the findings were promising. In summary, this research introduced a cutting-edge, bio-inspired technique for training SNNs and provided a practical solution for tackling real-world challenges. All the code used in this research is available online for the benefit of future development.

This research investigates the thermodynamic characteristics of spin-polarized strange quark matter under a strong magnetic field at finite temperature, applying the MIT bag model. We derived the spin-polarized strange quark matter equation of state for a strong magnetic field, considering the Landau levels of charged quarks. Furthermore, we determined the thermodynamic properties of spin-polarized strange quark matter, including its pressure, energy density, entropy density, heat capacity, magnetization, and spin polarization, as functions of temperature and the strength of the magnetic field. Our study revealed that the spin-polarized strange quark matter undergoes phase transitions from strange quark matter to strange hadron matter at specific critical temperatures, which depend on the strength of the magnetic field. Additionally, we found that the heat capacity of spin-polarized strange quark matter exhibits a cusp-like shape at these phase transition points. Notably, the heat capacity at these phase transition points is sensitive to the strength of the magnetic field and displays a cusp-like shape. Our findings are relevant to the study of spin-polarized strange quark matter in strong magnetic fields, present in the cores of neutron stars, and suggest that heat capacity measurements could serve as an indicator for detecting these magnetized neutron stars. Our results also provide theoretical predictions for future laboratory experiments involving high-energy particle collisions in strong magnetic fields. A 2-edge-connected and non-admissible 1-factorizable graph G is defined as a graph whose bipartite dual, B*, contains a perfect matching that corresponds to every edge in one of its partition sets. We have established the existence of an integer k ≥ 3, such that for every positive integer n, there exists a 2-edge-connected and non-admissible 1-factorizable graph G with n vertices whose bipartite dual B* contains at least k perfect matchings that cover every vertex in its partition sets. This result supplements previous findings by Chao and Hsu, and Chang and Kuo, and further extends their limits by increasing the number of vertices that such graphs can accommodate. Additionally, we have developed an infinite family of 2-edge-connected and non-admissible 1-factorizable graphs G with n vertices whose bipartite dual B* contains exactly n-1 perfect matchings that cover every vertex in one of its partition sets. Notably, these results provide an answer to a conjecture proposed by Chao and Hsu. The Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian property (PMH-property) in a graph G refers to the condition that there exists a Hamiltonian cycle in B* whose corresponding perfect matchings in B* cover every vertex in one of its partition sets. We have demonstrated the existence of an integer k ≥ 3, such that for every positive integer n, there exists a graph G with n vertices that satisfies the PMH-property, thereby confirming a previous conjecture by Chao and Hsu and extending the previously established limits by an unlimited amount. Moreover, we have created an infinite family of graphs G with n vertices that satisfy the PMH-property, meeting the requirements of a previous conjecture by Chao and Hsu. Both of these outcomes were achieved without relying on the use of either the Discrete Logarithm Problem or the Integer Factorization Problem. Instead, the results were obtained through the development of novel and direct approaches to constructing graphs with the desired properties. These methods are distinct from the previously established techniques in the field. Systematically constructing graphs G with specific properties was made possible by the introduction of a new and general framework that combines the use of both the Steinhaus-Haggertys Construction and the Bigs-Bigs Construction. This framework enables the creation of graphs G with n vertices that satisfy the 2-edge-connected and non-admissible 1-factorizable condition, as well as the PMH-property, for any given positive integer n. This paper introduces Timeloops, a lightweight, high-performance system call filtering framework designed for containerized applications. System call filtering is a critical security feature that helps prevent malicious code from causing harm, but existing solutions struggle to balance precision and speed. To address this challenge, we developed Timeloops, a static binary analysis tool that generates minimal, precise filters for taintdumper, a high-speed system call filtering engine. In contrast to static analysis-based techniques, Timeloops produces significantly smaller filter files and analysis times are substantially shorter. To evaluate the effectiveness of Timeloops, we conducted a series of experiments using real-world applications and malicious programs. The results showed that Timeloops outperforms the Linux Audit framework in terms of precision, recall, and system call filtering speed. Furthermore, our analysis revealed that the source code of popular programming languages, such as Go, Java, and Python, requires specific handling to accurately determine system calls, and we have made corresponding patches publicly available. To facilitate further research and improve system call filtering, we have released Timeloops as an open-source framework. In addition, we have created a system call dataset for containerized applications, which includes over 1.5 million system calls from real-world applications and containerized environments. This dataset can be accessed through our website. In summary, Timeloops offers a more efficient and accurate solution for system call filtering in containerized applications. In particular, it provides a more effective filtering solution for taintdumper, and its system call dataset can be beneficial for various machine learning applications. This paper introduces a Poisson multi-Bernoulli mixture (PMBM) filter where target appearance probabilities are organized on a grid, reducing the number of variables to be tracked and managed. Compared to traditional implementations using Gaussian mixture models, the proposed method significantly decreases the computational load and memory requirements. A linearization technique is employed to convert the Gaussian mixture density to a grid-based representation, enabling the application of standard prediction and update equations. The efficacy of this approach is demonstrated through simulations of static and moving targets in cluttered environments. Results show that the proposed method achieves comparable estimation performance to Gaussian mixture models at a lower computational cost. Moreover, the method offers improved scalability to large-scale target tracking scenarios. A motion compensation method is also presented to enhance the dynamic target tracking experience. The presented algorithm and its variants are suitable for various real-world target tracking applications. The code is available online for further customization.

We investigate the spectral stability of solitary waves from two different models: the Klein-Gordon equation and the Klein-Gordon-Schrodinger system. For the Klein-Gordon equation, we examine a one-dimensional, single-component model and its equivalent variational form. These forms enable us to establish both lower and upper bounds for the spectrum of linearized operators around solitary waves, thereby determining their spectral stability. Furthermore, we find that for a specific parameter value, this model exhibits a bifurcation point where a pair of purely imaginary eigenvalues emerge, indicating the coexistence of solitary waves and periodic solutions along the branch of solitary waves. This result is particularly significant because it provides an analytical explanation for the phenomenon observed in numerical simulations, where a solitary wave eventually breaks into multiple periodic solutions over time. In contrast, we also analyze a previous study claiming the existence of a threshold for wave speeds below which solitary waves are unstable, finding instead that the true criterion for stability is the presence of a positive eigenvalue, in turn determined by the presence or absence of a branch of periodic solutions in the solution space. In addition, we extend our analysis to a higher-dimensional Klein-Gordon equation, the results of which indicate that the condition of positive eigenvalues can be satisfied in either the one-dimensional periodic case or the one-dimensional solitary wave case, but not in the two-dimensional solitary wave case. In the context of the Klein-Gordon-Schrodinger system, we establish the existence and uniqueness of solitary wave solutions, as well as their variational structure, but the corresponding linearized operator does not possess compact resolvents due to the failure of compactness of the embedding of the phase space of the Schrodinger component. Consequently, we cannot determine the spectral stability of these solutions using the method employed for the Klein-Gordon equation. Instead, we apply a different approach based on the integrated density of states, which enables us to draw conclusions about the spectral stability of these solutions. Ultimately, we find that the solitary wave solutions of the Klein-Gordon-Schrodinger system are spectrally stable, whereas the system's system's branch of periodic solutions exhibits positive eigenvalues, indicating that these solutions are unstable. In addition, we investigate a modified Klein-Gordon-Schrodinger system in both one and two dimensions, for which we establish the existence of solutions that correspond to either solitary waves or periodic solutions along any given branch, as well as the conditions under which a branch of solutions changes from being stable to unstable, or vice versa. The rise of Artificial Intelligence has led to various applications, including both cloud and mobile services, where streamlined processes and efficient information management are crucial. Despite advancements in image processing, many organizations still rely on manual methods to extract information from scanned documents, including ID cards. To address this challenge, a system was developed that utilizes a deep learning technique called Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) in conjunction with Optical Character Recognition (OCR) software to accurately capture ID card data from images. Initially, the system was trained on 300 Indian ID card images and later expanded to 3000 images from various sources, resulting in a 94% accuracy rate in reading data with the OCR tool. To enhance the system's versatility, it was further trained to adapt to new ID cards without a significant drop in performance. The developed framework can be applied to other types of ID cards by adjusting its training data. To make the system more user-friendly, a mobile application was created that enables ID card holders to submit their documents simply by taking a photo, without the need for any additional data entry. The system's effectiveness is demonstrated through a cloud-based service where over 5000 ID cards were processed with a 99.5% accuracy rate within a 6-month period. To facilitate widespread adoption, the system's source code was made available on an open-source platform. The developed solution can be utilized by various organizations, both privately owned and government-operated, to streamline their document management processes. The system's potential applications extend beyond ID cards to any document that contains text, and can be especially beneficial to industries that handle a large volume of scanned documents. The system's ability to adapt to new documents without a significant decrease in accuracy makes it an ideal solution for cloud-based services. The source code of the developed framework is available on GitHub at the link: https://github.com/rahulraut/ID-Card-Reader. The mobile application is available for download on Google Play Store at the link: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.idreader.idreader. The system's cloud-based service can be accessed through its website at the link: https://idreader.com/. The data used to train the system is available on Kaggle at the link: https://www.kaggle.com/rahulraut/id-card-images. The system's performance can be replicated by training the CNN model on a dataset of 3000 ID card images, using the ResNet50 architecture with a learning rate of 0.001 and a batch size of 32

Calculations of position expectations were carried out for multiple scenarios of mass, angular frequency, and the lambda parameter in both cases. Constant driving led to coherent states, with theoretical predictions closely matched by both simulation approaches. A discrete-time lattice Metropolis algorithm was used to evaluate the imaginary time path integral for these simulations. As the number of time steps increased, more accurate results were obtained, with simulations limited by computational memory rather than accuracy. A comparison of simulation methods revealed similar performance, with the sampling efficiency of the lattice algorithm comparable to the continuous-time method. However, the lattice algorithm had an advantage in sampling the distribution of the position variable, as demonstrated by its ability to accurately capture the distribution of position variables for both small and large amplitude vibrations. Additionally, the algorithm allowed for the simulation of a wider range of mass values, extending to very small masses where the sampling of the position variable is highly non-uniform, requiring a more sophisticated sampling method to achieve efficient sampling. The Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effect significantly impacts the rotation of small asteroids by exerting a gentle, solar-powered torque. This phenomenon is particularly evident in asteroids with extremely slow or stopped rotations. To better understand the YORP effect and its influence on these asteroids, it is essential to precisely determine their rotation periods. However, this task becomes increasingly difficult as rotation periods lengthen, making it hard to identify them beyond a 24-hour limit. To address this challenge, we developed a new method for determining long rotation periods by utilizing a frequency analysis of data from stellar occultations. This approach was successfully applied to 15 asteroids with suspected YORP-related characteristics, and their rotation periods were determined with a high degree of accuracy. The observed period range extends from 10.8 hours to 67.8 hours, and our results are supported by theoretical models of the YORP effect. Ultimately, this research provides a practical tool for detecting and studying slow-rotating asteroids and sheds light on the YORP effect's critical role in their evolution. Additionally, our findings contribute to a growing database of rotation periods for asteroids and highlight the value of precise period measurements in constraining YORP-related timescales. To achieve this, we developed a new algorithm for estimating rotation periods and tested its efficacy using simulated data sets of varying complexity. The performance of this algorithm was found to be highly effective in recovering original periods, even in the presence of significant noise, and its application to real data from stellar occultations is promising. The resulting set of 15 studied asteroids with determined rotation periods offers valuable insights into their physical characteristics and behavior. The study of these asteroids reveals a distinct population with short ejection velocities from their parent bodies, suggesting that the YORP effect has a significant impact on their evolution over time scales of millions to tens of millions of years. The observed period distribution of these asteroids is consistent with predictions made by YORP-related models of their evolution. In contrast, homeomorphisms of the circle whose action within the interval $(-1,1)$ exhibits a similar level of complexity are found to be conditionally compact. We demonstrate that regular functions with computable inverses can be implemented using linear time computations on trees, thereby establishing that these functions conform to a specific subclass of continuous functions that can be defined using linear time computability along trees. This classification is distinct from other categories of functions with computable inverses, such as polynomial time computable invertible functions and modular functions with invertible counterparts, which exhibit different levels of computability when evaluated on trees. Our proof strategy involves examining the structural characteristics of regular languages with invertible elements and demonstrating that they can be represented using symmetrical regular automata, and in turn, these automata have equivalent descriptions as tree automata with specific rewriting rules, including regular tree rewriting rules with invertible functions, structural tree rewriting rules, and nested word rewriting rules. Furthermore, we show that these equivalent descriptions enable the computation of these regular functions within linear time, thereby establishing the connection between linear time computability along trees and the specified class of regular functions with invertible elements. Additionally, our research contributes to the understanding of other regular languages with unique properties, including those with specific levels of regularity, those that are recognizable by tree automata with a specific number of counters, and those that have specific levels of symmetry, and provides a theoretical framework for examining these characteristics using a combination of formal language theory and the theory of tree automata. This framework is then applied to provide a new characterization of regular functions with invertible elements, thereby expanding the set of functions that belong to the P system mentioned in the paper referenced below, and in turn, this characterization enables the verification of the computability of specific P systems, and in particular, enables the confirmation that the P system described in the paper referenced below is indeed computationally universal. This confirmation is significant because the original claim of the paper referenced below was met with skepticism by the universal computation theory community. This confirmation is achieved by demonstrating that the specified class of regular functions with invertible elements has a matching equivalent definition that is more aligned with the original intentions of the paper referenced below, and in turn, this matching definition provides the necessary evidence to support the claim made in the paper referenced below. This achievement is made possible by the previously mentioned research contributions of the current paper. A machine learning technique called next-generation reservoir computing overcomes limitations of traditional reservoir computing, resulting in significantly faster training and improved performance. This improved model leverages a complex neural network to accurately predict time series data from a compressed version of its past, and applies this advancement to a recent dataset from a photonic system. When put up against traditional methods, next-generation reservoir computing demonstrates a substantial reduction in required training data and enhanced prediction accuracy. Furthermore, its applicability to a photonic system allows for a speed boost in both training and prediction tasks. Our latest model includes two key enhancements: a way to determine the ideal number of nodes in the system and a method to enhance prediction results. These enhancements are shown to improve performance in a real-world dataset related to wind power forecasting. Our code is available online for public use.

The ventral temporal cortex's animacy organization is not binary, as it also differentiates animal species from one another. We investigated this continuum further by using a categorization task to analyze functional data from seven individuals with average resolution MRI scans. Two non-binary hypotheses were considered: animals are arranged along a continuum based on their ecological niches and species that are similar in appearance are grouped together. Our findings from the MRI scans support the latter hypothesis, revealing that the VTC's animacy structure is influenced by the visual characteristics of animals. This was confirmed by statistically analyzing the distribution of features that define different animal categories. We also found that the VTC's response is correlated with the visual similarity of animals, using a functional similarity matrix derived from the data. This correlation was observed across multiple ROIs and was more pronounced when comparing mammals with birds and other animals. Our results provide a foundation for exploring the neural basis of animal categorization and suggest that the VTC's response is closely tied to the visual characteristics of animals, even within a continuum of animacy. This was demonstrated by using a machine learning model to classify animals based on the VTC's response and the features used in our analysis. Our approach and findings can be applied to understanding the neural basis of animal categorization in other populations, such as individuals with synesthesia, and to developing more effective machine learning models for animal classification. Our code and data are available online at the following repository: https://github.com/zhengyin93/animal-continuum-VTC.

We have adapted the quantum relational Hoare logic originally proposed by Brodsky and Pugh to accommodate "expectations" within its preconditions and postconditions, thereby enabling the quantification of pre- and post-relational properties that reflect the program's efficiency. This extension, however, necessitates a more rigorous definition of postconditions and a modified proof rule for sequential programs. Furthermore, we have investigated the relationship between these expectations when applying the Hoare logic to quantum programs that utilize storage variables. Our examination also includes an examination of four example programs. Finally, we have established the equivalence between our expectation-based approach and the original quantum relational Hoare logic, providing a proof of the soundness of our expectation-based framework in relation to the original specification. Our extension of the quantum relational Hoare logic has implications for the verification of quantum programs that measure and manage costs, as well as those that leverage garbage collection. Our expectation-based approach offers a promising direction for developing a Hoare logic that can effectively handle performance-related specifications within the verification of quantum programs. Our approach is also amenable to the verification of classical programs with performance-related specifications. Our findings are part of a broader research effort that aims to bridge the gap between formal verification and testing for quantum programs, as well as to explore the potential benefits of performance-aware verification for quantum programs. The rapid spread of infectious diseases is influenced by various factors, including the number of people in close contact with each other and the efficiency with which an individual transmits the disease to others. We developed a compound Poisson epidemic model that takes into account super-spreader events, which have a significant impact, and found that the model's average infection rate, or $R_0$, can be much higher than expected, varying inversely with the square root of the number of contacts. When we applied this model to a scenario with many contacts, we found that it resulted in a value of $R_0$ that far exceeded the critical threshold of one, and could lead to outbreaks becoming epidemics. Furthermore, we used the model to simulate the spread of a disease within a network of interconnected groups, and discovered that the model accurately captured the effects of super-spreader events on the speed of their spread, as well as the impact of altering the number of contacts each person has with others. We also found that this model could be used to assess the effectiveness of public health policies aimed at controlling the spread of a disease. We further developed the compound Poisson model into a continuous-time model that can be used to study the spread of a disease within a large population over time, and used this model to investigate the long-term outcomes of different public health policies, and found that those that reduced the average number of contacts each person had with others were the most effective at preventing the spread of a disease. We also found that the introduction of super-spreader events could cause a sudden and significant increase in the number of people infected with a disease, and that public health policies aimed at reducing the impact of these events must take into account the number of people in close contact with each other. We further developed this continuous-time model into a stochastic version that can be used to study the spread of a disease within a large and complex network of interconnected groups over time, and used this model to investigate the long-term outcomes of different public health policies aimed at controlling the spread of a disease, and found that the most effective policies were those that reduced the average number of contacts each person had with others, and that these policies were more effective when applied to networks with super-spreader events. We've developed a statistical approach to assess the bias in estimating the component of the magnetic field that's perpendicular to our line-of-sight, taking into consideration various observational limitations. Taking into account the distribution of current sheet thickness, Alfvén critical radius, and the size of magnetic flux tubes, along with the properties of turbulent plasma behavior, we used a statistical model to estimate this component of the magnetic field, denoted as $B_\perp$. Our method accounts for the incomplete sampling of strong magnetic fields within turbulent plasma and allows us to estimate the bias in measuring $B_\perp$ as 1.66 times, along with an uncertainty of 0.66. This is particularly relevant for studying local magnetic fields within the solar corona. If we apply this method to previous measurements of coronal field strengths, it suggests that the missing component of the magnetic field could be overestimated by a factor of two, which has implications for our understanding of magnetic energy within the solar corona. Additionally, this approach highlights the limitations of using the Poynting vector to quantify magnetic energy within the corona. Monte Carlo simulations encounter a "sign problem" when sampling configurations with a given weight that depends on the phase of a complex quantity. This sign problem worsens as the system deviates from half-filling, hindering Monte Carlo calculations, particularly for discrete, anisotropic, and discrete Kondo lattice models. We have developed a novel Monte Carlo algorithm that addresses this issue by sampling the phase of a complex, anisotropically weighted average of local occupation numbers. This algorithm allows for efficient Monte Carlo simulations of the discrete Kondo lattice model, even at low temperatures, and facilitates the determination of spectral functions. For the anisotropic Dirac hubbard model, we have developed a related Monte Carlo method that generates correlated random numbers, both within and between different spatial locations, enabling the simulation of an anisotropic sign problem. This has important implications for Monte Carlo simulations of anisotropic lattice models near a Dirac point, and we demonstrate the accuracy and efficiency of these methods by simulating the anisotropic Dirac hubbard model and comparing the resulting spectral functions with exact diagonalization data. Furthermore, we have applied these methods to study an anisotropic Dirac hubbard model along a line of critical end points in the phase diagram of an interacting one-dimensional chain that is coupled to a one-dimensional bath, and we have obtained the resulting phase diagram. This includes a new, incommensurate antiferromagnetic phase that is separated from a dimerized phase by a tricritical point, and we have found that this tricritical point lies along a line that extends from a well-known tricritical point at half-filling, and it ends at a filling that is one-third of the total lattice sites. This tricritical point is characterized by a universal tricritical behavior, and it controls the anisotropic scaling of the associated tricritical exponent, and it also determines the filling dependence of the associated tricritical temperature. This has significant implications for understanding the physics of an interacting one-dimensional chain that is coupled to a one-dimensional bath, particularly when the bath is a fermionic bath that is described by the Hubbard-Hubbard model. This includes the full range of fillings from half-filling to one-third filling, and it includes the associated phase diagrams, energy spectra, and anisotropic correlation functions. By leveraging previously acquired skills and adapting them to unfamiliar tasks without explicit guidance, humans demonstrate exceptional cross-task capabilities.
This study aims to enhance the cross-task generalization ability of massive language models in unsupervised settings, with a focus on models like T0 and FLAN.
We introduce a novel, unsupervised retrieval-augmentation method called Target Task Predictor (TTP) that improves cross-task performance by identifying relevant past tasks and retrieving their supervised data, without requiring access to task annotations.
In addition to TTP, we introduce a set of techniques to enhance performance, including a co-training strategy and a semi-supervised training method using pseudo-labels, which we collectively refer to as Target Task Augmentation (TTA).
Our TTA framework can be applied to various unsupervised retrieval-augmentation methods, not just TTP.
Across 7 diverse text generation tasks, our model exhibits improved performance when pre-trained with TTA, achieving a significant 12% increase in F1-score over the current state-of-the-art, while our method also demonstrates robust performance in a real-world application, where it reduces the gap to a human-like performance by 50%. Our code and pre-trained models are available at https://github.com/THUcrossAI/TargetTaskAug.

Optimizing hyperparameters in the private version of the stochastic gradient descent algorithm is a complex task due to the limited amount of data and the introduction of randomization to protect privacy. To address this challenge, we investigate several optimization techniques for varying the hyperparameters of a privately learned linear regression model. Our findings, validated through extensive experiments, reveal that two algorithms stand out in terms of effectiveness: Cross Validation with a small number of iterations, and Grid Search with a larger number of iterations. We observed that these two methods yield comparable performance in a private setting, both outperforming the conventional hold-out method. To further enhance the accuracy of private machine learning, we propose a novel approach called Adaptive Regularized Cross Validation, which incorporates an optimized regularized cross-validation algorithm to adapt the model to varying data sets. Experimentation with real-world data demonstrates the efficacy of this method in achieving a balance between model complexity and the degree of privacy. Our results also highlight the significance of carefully selecting the number of iterations in various optimization techniques, as well as the relationship between the number of iterations and the level of privacy. For a Coxeter system denoted by (W,S), we develop the concept of a boolean complex consisting of involutions within W, mirroring Ragnarsson and Tenner's previous work. By applying discrete Morse theory, we identify the homotopy type of this boolean complex for a significant subset of Coxeter groups, including finite groups, revealing that its homotopy type is equivalent to that of a collection of spheres with dimension |S|-1. Specifically, we demonstrate that for a Coxeter group with any number of generators greater than 2, its boolean complex has a homotopy type equivalent to a single sphere of the same dimension. This extends and refines earlier results by Ragnarsson and Tenner, as well as Armstrong and Miller, by broadening the group coefficients from finite to general coefficients. Moreover, we derive formulas for calculating the Euler characteristic of the boolean complex, providing a comparison with existing methods. Furthermore, we introduce the notion of a standard boolean complex and establish its connection to the weak order, along with a formula for its Euler characteristic. Finally, we examine the properties of a Coxeter group's boolean complex when generated by two elements, demonstrating its connection to the braid graph and presenting the Euler characteristic of the associated sphere as 1. This research was initially presented at the 2018 International Conference on Coxeter Groups held in Salt Lake City, Utah. We applied an advanced statistical approach to examine variations in elemental abundances within nearby stars using a massive dataset of 49,881 stellar spectra. A two-component model was employed to capture similarities and differences between abundances in prompt and delayed supernovae, respectively. This resulted in an extensive database of 24 chemical elements, along with associated uncertainties, and their ranges within the local stellar population. Prompt supernovae were found to account for the majority of elements, except for iron-group elements, neutron-capture elements, and nickel, which were attributed to delayed supernovae. Estimates of abundance ranges were calculated and used to assess the distribution of variables, ultimately shedding light on the composition of prompt and delayed supernovae. Furthermore, this study revealed an inverse correlation between silicon and oxygen abundances and provided a possible explanation for this phenomenon, potentially linked to the properties of massive stars that give rise to prompt supernovae. This comprehensive database of elemental abundances can be applied to various astrophysical contexts, including the study of supernovae remnants, chemical enrichment models, and the evolution of nearby star clusters. This analysis also highlights the significance of spectroscopic parallaxes in reducing the dispersion of abundance variables and, in turn, improving the understanding of supernovae that shape the local chemical environment. The rapid transmission and evolution of online rumors pose significant challenges in public health crises. This study aims to provide quantitative insights into the spread of COVID-19-related rumors on Weibo, using data from the Chinese National Rumor Control Center. We gather and verify 1470 rumors that circulated in China during the initial two months of the pandemic and analyze factors contributing to their popularity. Our findings reveal that the spread of a rumor is influenced by its content, and how it relates to specific locations, events, and figures in the community. We also observe that the spread of a rumor is more extensive in areas with severe pandemic restrictions, and that it peaks one to two weeks after the initial outbreak in that region. Furthermore, our analysis shows that the spread of a rumor is correlated with the number of new cases in the following two to three weeks. We use these insights to develop a statistical model that predicts the spread of a rumor over time, and demonstrate its effectiveness using cross-validation. Our results highlight the importance of addressing the root causes of a public health crisis, and the need for real-time, geographically-specific information to combat the spread of online rumors. Our model also provides a framework for evaluating interventions aimed at controlling the spread of a rumor. Our study's methodology and findings can be applied to other public health crises, and other social media platforms. Our model is available online for further development and testing. Physiological big data processing requires an advanced framework that can efficiently handle large amounts of streaming physiological signals while providing reliable and secure cloud computing capabilities. To address the limitations of existing data processing solutions, we present LifeStream, a dedicated framework for processing physiological big data in the cloud. LifeStream is distinguished by its ability to process continuous, high-density streaming data efficiently, leveraging Hadoop's MapReduce architecture and ETL (Extract, Transform, Load) processing methods. Furthermore, LifeStream is equipped with a data validation module to ensure data accuracy and a cloud security module to safeguard against unauthorized data access. In comparison to traditional streaming engines and cloud data processing platforms, LifeStream offers superior performance and data management capabilities. Our experimental results demonstrate LifeStream's superior performance in processing large-scale physiological data streams across multiple cloud platforms. Specifically, LifeStream achieves significant improvements in processing speed, data management efficiency, and security features. In addition, we outline potential applications and future directions for LifeStream in processing physiological big data in cloud environments. The LifeStream framework is available for public use on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/PhysioSense/ LifeStream. In summary, LifeStream provides a comprehensive and adaptable framework for processing large-scale physiological data streams in cloud environments, offering valuable benefits for various research fields and real-world scenarios. The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, little research has been conducted to examine the impact of loss function on the performance of neural networks in supervised classification tasks. In an attempt to address this knowledge gap, this study undertakes an exhaustive evaluation of loss functions for neural networks, presenting an empirical analysis of 17 commonly employed loss functions across six distinct classification problems. The study reveals that many loss functions, although derived from probabilistic models, can be effectively utilized with deterministic neural networks, suggesting that the term "likelihood" in some loss function names may be misleading. Furthermore, this study finds that the widely accepted classification loss functions mean squared error and cross-entropy yield comparable performance, leaving the selection between them to be arbitrary. Consequently, this research encourages the development of new loss functions based on the underlying mechanics of neural networks, rather than probabilistic theory. In addition, the study's open-source code enables other researchers to reproduce the results and extend the evaluation to emerging loss functions. This research is relevant to the community working on deep learning and supervised classification. The associated code can be accessed at https://github.com/zhenghua333/loss_function_analysis.

The mechanical and thermal behavior of crystalline regions within stretched polymer materials has been extensively studied, yet its fundamental theoretical basis remains unclear. To address this, we developed a multi-scale model that combines finite element method simulations at both molecular and crystalline levels to capture strain-induced crystallization. This model then was utilized to analyze the mechanical and thermal responses of polymer materials undergoing crystallization. As a result, we found that crystallization leads to an increase in mechanical stiffness and a decrease in thermal expansion. Furthermore, to validate our approach, we compared our model with existing strain-induced crystallization models and found that it aligns with their mechanical predictions. Notably, our multi-scale model revealed that crystallization causes thermal expansion coefficients to vary with strain levels, a phenomenon not previously observed. To verify our findings, we conducted experiments on polypropylene tape under uniaxial tension and stretching, which showed a corresponding decrease in thermal expansion coefficients with increasing strain. Our research thus provides a mechanistic explanation for the observed thermal expansion behavior of polymer materials during crystallization. To facilitate practical applications, we developed a simplified model that can be used to predict thermal expansion coefficients based on material composition and processing conditions. Our study's outcomes are relevant to various fields, including materials science, polymer engineering, and geophysics, and its findings can be used to develop new materials and improve existing manufacturing processes. To facilitate this, we made our code publicly available. Our research revealed that thermal expansion coefficients can be controlled through crystallization-induced anisotropy, leading to a significant reduction of up to 30%. Our results also showed that draw ratio and molecular weight influence the thermal expansion behavior of polymer materials during stretching. To analyze the impact of an external magnetic field on doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ with spin-triplet nematic superconductivity, a fully self-consistent London-type model is employed in a vector London equation formulation, accounting for the anisotropic nature of the abovementioned superconducting state. The effects of the anisotropic superconducting gap are particularly emphasized in the analysis. It is observed that the magnetic field induces a shift in the orientation of the nematic superconducting state's long axis, and this anisotropic behavior can result in the destruction of superconductivity at a lower critical field than an isotropic scenario. Moreover, the lower critical field's anisotropy is linked to the anisotropic nature of the energy gap, and this anisotropy is found to influence the London penetration depth's anisotropy. As a result, the anisotropic nature of the energy gap must be considered when interpreting experimental data featuring a unidirectional in-plane applied magnetic field. Additionally, the model reveals that the London penetration depth's anisotropy can be used to determine the spin-triplet component of the energy gap. The model's predictions are relevant to the study of HgTe-based quantum wells and other doped topological insulators. The anisotropic nature of the energy gap can be directly confirmed by inelastic neutron scattering, and this method is recommended for use in future experiments. The model's limitations and potential extensions are also discussed. The predicted anisotropic behavior of the London penetration depth's anisotropy suggests that the search for spin-triplet superconductivity in doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ should be expanded to include studies of bulk samples with unidirectional applied magnetic fields. The model's implications for the study of vortex lattice states in spin-triplet superconductors are also explored. The predicted anisotropic behavior of the vortex lattice's structure and orientation is confirmed, and this anisotropy is linked to the anisotropic nature of the energy gap. The model's predictions for the vortex lattice's behavior are consistent with those obtained using a combination of the Ginzburg-Landau free energy functional and the relaxation method. The anisotropic nature of the energy gap's components can be used to determine the orientation of the vortex lattice's long axis. The model's predictions for the vortex lattice's behavior are relevant to the study of HgTe-based quantum wells and other doped topological insulators.

The study of quantum systems' behavior through the analysis of energy histograms is a fundamental approach. At thermal equilibrium, thermodynamic quantities like the thermodynamic width, variance of energy, specific heat, and quantum work distribution width measure fluctuations of energy density relative to the mean. Investigating these quantities is crucial for understanding both closed and closed-and-open quantum systems. In this paper, we examine the width of the variance of energy, a quantity that has not been extensively studied in the literature, and derive its expression in terms of the total system's Hamiltonian and its interactions with the surroundings. We also demonstrate that in certain scenarios, the variance of energy density can be expressed in a simplified form that has previously been established numerically. Notably, we find that in contact with a thermal bath, the variance of energy density is solely determined by its temperature and the system's quantum properties. Moreover, we provide explicit expressions for its derivatives with respect to time, average energy, and temperature, offering valuable insights into its behavior over time, in equilibrium, and away from equilibrium. These findings are further illustrated through numerical simulations of various quantum systems connected to a thermal bath. The study presented here provides a comprehensive foundation for exploring more complex open quantum systems and their applications in quantum thermodynamics. The research also sheds light on the relationship between the variance of energy density and other related quantities, revealing a linear relationship with the system's quantum work distribution width and the variance of the work done on the system. The results obtained can be utilized in the investigation of quantum systems' behavior in various scenarios, including those with periodic driving forces or non-equilibrium conditions. The study's findings are expected to contribute to the development of quantum thermodynamics and its applications in quantum technology and quantum thermophysics. For example, it can identify that "drinking coffee" leads to "feeling awake." Portfolio optimization is a critical task in finance that can be computationally intensive, but when accomplished using the HHL quantum algorithm, with its speedup, can be remarkably efficient. However, achieving meaningful performance enhancements with the HHL algorithm on current-day intermediate-scale quantum computers is challenging due to their limited size compared to the massive matrix dimensions required for portfolio optimization. In response to this limitation, we developed a novel, compact representation of the type-I Tobin's Q matrix, taking advantage of the machine's native memory structure, and applied a range of quantum data compression techniques to compress the matrix, taking into account its inherent low-rank properties. As a result, we successfully executed a portfolio optimization task on a 53-qubit quantum computer within reasonable error tolerance, exceeding the capabilities of classical devices for several orders of magnitude. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that the HHL algorithm's performance can be significantly improved by leveraging the matrix's inherent structure and low-rank properties, and our approach offers a versatile framework that can be applied to various applications beyond portfolio optimization. Specifically, our approach yields a low-rank representation of the Tobin's Q matrix at an estimated 10 to the power of 20, allowing us to execute the algorithm on a 53-qubit quantum device with an estimated 500 times improvement over classical devices. Our research demonstrates the practical value of the HHL algorithm in real-world settings and highlights the benefits of using quantum computers for portfolio optimization, including a 2 orders of magnitude reduction in shot count and estimated execution time of 1.5 hours on a 53-qubit quantum device, as well as a 500 times increase in the size of the portfolio. Our code is available at https://github.com/QuantumPortfolioOptimization/QPO. Our findings were presented at the 2023 IEEE International Conference on Quantum Science and Technology. To enhance data efficiency of state-of-the-art end-to-end ASR models and enable them to utilize visual information effectively, a method has been proposed for multimodal training using masked visual representations. This approach overcomes two significant obstacles hindering the widespread adoption of multimodal ASR: ensuring that models can generalize to unmasked inputs and handling the challenge of finding a suitable alignment between spoken and visual data. Our proposed solution involves leveraging a self-supervised vision model that generates a set of context-based masked visual representations, and employs a multi-task ASR model that simultaneously predicts both the ASR transcript and the visual context from the encoded speech signal. This study examines the long-term behavior of a randomly generated uniform parking distribution, denoted as P_n, with the focus on its initial k_n positions. To characterize how these early places influence the distribution's long-term behavior, we establish that P_n's limit resembles a stationary, irreducible Markov chain, whose initial k_n states act as a coordinating class. This conclusion is based on an in-depth analysis of the random uniform distribution's properties and ergodic theory. Specifically, we apply the asymptotic properties of the sum of the first k_n places in P_n to show that its limit forms a Markov chain with a coordinating class, and this result generalizes an earlier finding by Diaconis and Hicks. Moreover, we derive explicit formulas for key distribution-related quantities, including the average of the first k_n places, which reveals a surprising connection to the harmonic series and its approximation by the Euler-Maclaurin formula. This connection enables us to estimate the asymptotic behavior of these averages as k_n grows proportionally to n. Finally, we explore analogous questions and obtain corresponding insights for randomly generated uniform parking functions with specific constraints, including those with fixed leading places and those without forbidden spaces. This research builds upon the foundation established by Diaconis and Hicks in their study of the Markov chain representing the sum of a randomly generated uniform parking function. This work also extends the findings of Diaconis and Hicks by considering the random uniform distribution's limit as its initial k_n places become increasingly distant from the coordinating class that defines its long-term behavior. This extension allows us to generalize their results and uncover new information about the random uniform distribution's asymptotic behavior. In addition, we uncover a previously unknown relationship between the average of the first k_n places in a randomly generated uniform parking function and the harmonic series, which we then use to explore the connections between these averages as k_n grows proportionally to n. This research further explores the connections between the random uniform distribution's asymptotic behavior and its initial places, which we discovered are governed by a Markov chain with a coordinating class, and provides a general framework for studying the random uniform distribution's properties in the limit as its initial places become increasingly distant from the coordinating class that defines its long-term behavior. Measurements of superconducting nanowires, specifically NbN nanowires, reveal the occurrence of an unusual quasiperiodic oscillation in voltage fluctuations during microwave excitation, particularly at low biases and within the superconducting critical regime. This behavior was observed over a broad frequency range, extending from a few kilohertz to several gigahertz, and its amplitude was found to be directly proportional to the applied microwave power. It is proposed that this quasiperiodic fluctuation pattern is attributed to quasiperiodic quasiparticle populations becoming unstable, and could be a manifestation of quasiparticle interference. This phenomenon may also contribute to the reported blockade of direct current conduction in superconducting nanowires. As a result, we anticipate that quasiparticle-related phenomena will play a significant role in the development of superconducting nanowire sensors, particularly those utilizing the energy resolution required for photon counting. Additionally, this discovery may lead to the creation of quasiperiodic quasiparticle-based oscillators with unique frequency modulation capabilities. As for the nanowire devices, their improved performance in low-bias applications is expected. This research was carried out by utilizing a single nanowire devices, but we suggest that quasiparticle-related phenomena will persist in nanowire sensors even after array optimization. Airborne transmission risk in confined environments is significantly impacted by the behavior of respiratory aerosols. Given the importance of accurately predicting these phenomena, we developed a multi-phase computational model that accounts for turbulent airflow and the transport of aerosols within the respiratory system. This model was applied to study the distribution of virus-carrying aerosols produced during coughing in various settings, including public transportation and healthcare facilities. Our findings, which include detailed data on aerosol particle size and velocity, can be utilized in subsequent analyses of transmission risk and intervention effectiveness. In fact, we propose an expanded model that incorporates the effects of aerosol transport on the spread of respiratory infections. This model has been made available online to facilitate further research and potential adaptation for use in computational tools employed by public health policymakers. We examine the concept of Lipschitz continuity within the context of training neural networks and highlight its relevance to various fairness metrics. A key result indicates that enforcing Lipschitz constraints on a neural network can lead to overestimation in its predictive capabilities, resulting in a theorem that provides a computational analogue to a statement made by Koh and Liang. Building upon this foundation, we explore multiple fairness metrics that are influenced by the Lipschitz norm of a neural network, including balanced accuracy and a particular case of top-K accuracy, and present methods to integrate these metrics into the standard neural network training framework using regularizers. Furthermore, we establish the relationship between the Lipschitz norm and the number of neurons within a neural network, which facilitates a study on reducing the network's size while maintaining desired performance standards. To this end, we investigate two approaches: one that optimizes the network's size directly and another that leverages the Rebuffi et al. layered architecture, and both are demonstrated to yield improved balanced accuracy when considering a specific dataset. We also explore the application of our fairness framework to the task of adversarial training. All the code used in this research is publicly available at https://github.com/zhongyuan-liu/LipNetwork.

We investigate the possibility of lepton-flavour non-universality in certain processes at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). To this end, we focus on Drell-Yan dilepton and W boson production data, then utilize Bayesian inference to constrain "third-generation" vector leptoquark models, specifically in their $t$-channel scenarios. By applying a Markov Chain Monte Carlo method, we determine the model parameters' posterior distributions, from which we derive upper bounds on the mass of vector leptoquarks and calculate corresponding suppression factors for lepton flavours. Our findings indicate that at the 13 TeV LHC, vector leptoquarks with couplings to tau and bottom flavours can be ruled out up to production masses of 720 GeV for same-flavour quark pairs and 810 GeV for different-flavour pairs, given a suppression factor of approximately one for tau flavours and two for charged leptons. Our analysis highlights the significance of incorporating systematic neutrino transverse momentum corrections into simulations of W boson and dilepton events. Our study also emphasizes the potential of the LHC for discovering evidence of lepton-flavour non-universality within vector leptoquark physics. Our code is available online for further research.

To achieve this, a mathematical model needs to be refined to account for the complex interactions between glucose metabolism, neurotransmitter systems, and blood flow in the brain. This study presents a novel approach using a nonlinear filter method to estimate Kp from PET scans of the brain, and evaluates its performance using simulated data. A linguistic approach known as centering theory seeks to explain how coherence in conversations is maintained by focusing on the central entity. This theory was initially developed to analyze the syntactic and semantic properties of individual sentences within a conversation. However, its potential to account for the coherence of entire conversations has yet to be explored. Our research applies centering theory to a comprehensive analysis of an entire conversation by utilizing a set of structural rules that assign a degree of coherence to each sentence based on the central entity and the connection it shares with the preceding sentence. We then examine the coherence of an entire conversation by aggregating the coherence of its individual sentences. Our study is demonstrated using data from a reference dialogue from the DSTC7 Dialogue Understanding Task, specifically the "book talk" dialogue. We also introduce a new evaluation metric called the Coherence Score, which measures the degree to which the predicted topic aligns with the actual topic by considering the shift of the central entity and the connection between consecutive sentences. Our findings show that models pre-trained on BERT and RoBERTa achieve better performance than the baseline model, and that the coherence of the reference dialogue scores 0.83 on a 7-point scale. Our research also highlights the challenges posed by the "book talk" dialogue data, which is characterized by long chains of connected sentences with a topic shift for each new sentence. Our code is available online for public use. Our research suggests that improving coherence understanding will be crucial for advancing in tasks like dialogue state tracking, where the goal is to identify the current situation of a conversation. Our proposed Coherence Score metric can be applied to evaluate the coherence of discourse in various domains beyond the "book talk" dialogue, and our approach to modeling coherence can be applied to tasks like cross-turn classification in dialogue, where the goal is to classify the current situation of a conversation based on the conversation history. Results indicate that this approach can reduce positioning errors caused by signal variations and improve navigation experiences. Theoretical modeling of polymer brushes on curved surfaces requires a more complex analysis than on planar surfaces due to varying grafting density. Researchers have proposed various methods to accommodate this variation, yet many simulations fail to account for regions near the brush's root where polymers are no longer grafted. We have analytically examined the structure of polymer brushes on paraboloid surfaces, incorporating regions around the root where polymers are excluded from grafting, and found them to resemble the brush morphology on flat surfaces. Conditional GANs have demonstrated superior performance in tasks requiring the generation of specific classes. However, the choice of loss function significantly influences the generated output and, as a result, the classification responsibility is often shifted to the classifier rather than the discriminator. We propose an enhanced training method for the classifier using a multi-task loss function that incorporates a domain confusion loss, which we believe is beneficial for the classification task. Our approach yields a CGAN where the classifier and discriminator share a feature extractor, and the classifier employs the domain confusion loss in conjunction with the multi-task loss to achieve class-conditional generation. Our model's efficacy is validated through the generation of handwritten digits and faces, as well as the original classification tasks for MNIST and FER2013, respectively. Our results show that our method surpasses the current state-of-the-art in terms of both classification accuracy and the quality of generated samples. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhengzhenghan/CCGAN.
