Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and a non-invasive method like cardiac auscultation is an ideal starting point for diagnosis. However, auscultation alone may lead to disagreements between medical professionals, indicating the value of additional information. This research proposes a method that combines cardiac auscultation sounds with a non-invasive imaging technique, specifically photoplethysmography, to create a 2D map of sounds and flow velocities. This data is then fed into a deep learning model to predict the severity of heart valve conditions, specifically mitral stenosis. Experiments using a small dataset of 15 subjects showed that this approach outperformed traditional signal processing methods and related medical imaging-based deep learning models, achieving a correlation coefficient of 0.83 with echocardiogram readings. A larger study is recommended to confirm these findings and explore ways to integrate this method with established clinical assessment tools. Existing models were outperformed by a proposed simple architecture, suggesting that cardiac-specific designs are beneficial, and the need for more diverse training and validation datasets was highlighted. This work demonstrates the feasibility of using photoplethysmography in conjunction with cardiac auscultation for the deep learning-based analysis of heart valve conditions, and it presents a novel, cardiac-specific deep learning model that can be used for this purpose. This research provides a foundation for exploring more complex conditions, expanding the dataset, and integrating this method with established clinical assessment tools. This study is relevant to the medical community and provides a starting point for developing related technologies, and it is also applicable to the development of related technologies in the field of cardiac sound analysis. This research was conducted in accordance with ethical standards, and written consent was obtained from all participants. This work is part of a larger project that aims to develop a comprehensive system for the diagnosis and assessment of heart valve conditions based on photoplethysmography and cardiac auscultation. This system is designed to be accessible and can be utilized in low-resource settings. This study focuses on a switching control issue with regime change discontinuities, where the objective is to minimize costs while adhering to constraints and navigating through a changing environment. A key finding reveals that the optimal cost function can be represented as a value function associated with a system of stochastic differential equations, which includes both absolute value terms and equations with jumping processes. Furthermore, we developed an iterative method to compute the value function's derivatives along its gradient, and our approach also yields an explicit formula for the solution to a related system of partial differential equations. A key aspect of our method involves utilizing the absolute value terms to derive novel integration-by-parts identities that can be applied to both continuous and jumping processes. This research was motivated by an example related to an optimal switching problem involving two different regimes, where the cost function includes the absolute value of the difference between two state variables, and this example demonstrates how our results can be applied to a broad category of problems. This work was inspired by an absolute value-based target formulation commonly found in economic applications and control theory. This formulation includes a cost function with absolute value terms and a driving signal that varies over time, and it was shown that under certain conditions, this problem can be transformed into a type of problem that involves changing regimes, which in turn can be solved using the methods presented in this research. This approach provides a framework for addressing a wide range of optimal switching problems that involve changing regimes, which includes both continuous and jumping processes, and it also offers a value function representation that can be useful in solving related systems of partial and stochastic differential equations. We investigated the level of nonequilibrium (non-LTE) in the excitation of ground-state rotational lines of CO to better understand the temperature and density of molecular gas within galaxies. Based on theoretical and observational studies, we found that non-LTE effects are substantial, especially in low-density environments, and could misrepresent gas temperatures by overestimating them by 1-3 K and underestimating densities by a factor of 1.5. These errors are more pronounced when using single-point observations rather than spatially resolved data. To address this issue, we developed an empirical model to correct non-LTE excitation based on the C I fine structure line ratio and 12 CO (1-0) and (2-1) line ratios. By applying this correction to observations of the Sombrero galaxy, we found that temperatures derived from CO (1-0) and CO (2-1) lines decreased by approximately 2 K after accounting for non-LTE effects. Furthermore, we determined the CO (2-1)/CO (1-0) line ratio to be 0.85±0.05, which is consistent with theoretical predictions and suggests that the gas temperatures in the Sombrero galaxy are consistent with a two-phase medium comprising warm, dense gas and cooler, less dense gas. However, when considering the limited spatial resolution of current and near-future interferometric observations, we found that the CO (2-1)/CO (1-0) line ratio may also be influenced by the distribution of gas temperatures and densities within the line-of-sight. Consequently, we recommend using the J=1-0 transition of the 13 CO isotopologue as an alternative to improve the accuracy of temperature and density estimates in future studies. Additionally, we found that the CO (2-1)/CO (1-0) line ratio can be an indicator of the presence of active galactic nuclei feedback in galaxies. In the sequence reconstruction problem, the goal is to determine the least number of transmitted channels that can be used to accurately recover a transmitted sequence, given that each channel conveys a function of the transmitted sequence and is subject to certain constraints. We have investigated this problem within two distinct models. First, with respect to a general framework, we established an upper limit on the number of recoverable channels, which is equivalent to a condition for sequence reconstruction. Then, by applying this general framework to specific cases involving binary channels, we obtained insights into the maximum number of channels that can be used to reconstruct sequences of specific lengths. Additionally, our analysis revealed that certain binary channel networks are capable of reconstructing sequences of any length, thereby providing a fundamental characterization of such networks. Furthermore, we established a connection between the sequence reconstruction problem and the ability to accurately estimate the transmitted sequence based on a large enough number of channel outputs, which we found to be ten times the sequence length for binary channels. Notably, our research revealed that the maximum number of recoverable channels is directly related to the required sample size to achieve a certain level of estimation accuracy, thereby highlighting the fundamental trade-off between the complexity of transmitted sequences and the number of channels that can be used to convey them accurately. Our work also introduced a novel algorithm for estimating transmitted sequences from channel outputs, which we found to be particularly effective for applications involving short sequences and simple channel networks. Our research has far-reaching implications for various fields, including information theory, machine learning, and signal processing, and it has the potential to guide the development of efficient communication protocols and data compression algorithms. Our research findings have been validated through extensive numerical simulations and experimental results obtained using a random access protocol with binary channels. Our work on the sequence reconstruction problem has been applied to a broader concept known as the identifiability of signals from channel outputs, which is critical for developing communication protocols and signal processing algorithms that enable the accurate estimation of transmitted sequences and signals in various applications. Researchers anticipate that Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) experiments will be capable of detecting gravitational waves produced by individual supermassive black hole binaries moving in highly elliptical orbits. By comparing various methods for computing PTA signals from these binaries, our findings indicate that employing approximate analytic expressions yields the quickest computation, while more precise results can be obtained using post-Newtonian waveforms in quasi-Circular orbits. However, for highly elliptical orbits, we developed a novel approach that combines a phenomenological fitting model for the PTA signals and their derivatives, allowing for efficient and accurate determination of PTA parameters. This method, which we refer to as HELENA, enables the simulation of PTA signals from individual supermassive black hole binaries moving in highly elliptical orbits and facilitates efficient fitting of PTA data. HELENA's efficacy is demonstrated through the analysis of mock PTA datasets. Our study highlights the importance of accurately modeling PTA signals from extreme binary systems and the potential limitations of general relativistic precessions, as well as the necessity of correctly accounting for PTA instrumental noise. Our work also presents a comprehensive set of realistic PTA signal models, which can be utilized for testing alternative theories of gravity. Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for various applications, including flood risk assessment and water quality management. While computational fluid dynamics is a reliable method for solving the full Navier-Stokes equations, it is often impractical due to high computational costs for large-scale river networks. In contrast, shallow water equations provide a more computationally efficient alternative but may not accurately capture high-frequency velocity variations. This study combines the strengths of both approaches by developing a deep learning-based method that models river flow velocity patterns. We trained a convolutional neural network using data from the Yangtze River and found it effectively captured velocity oscillations, as evident from both numerical and experimental results. When applied to the same river network using SE3D, the learned model significantly improved velocity predictions, with a 30% reduction in error compared to SE3D alone. Furthermore, by integrating the machine learning model with SE3D, we achieved a 50% decrease in error when predicting velocities in an ungauged river segment. This study demonstrates the effectiveness of a machine learning-based model in predicting river flow velocities with high-frequency components and highlights its potential for large-scale river network applications. HDR photography combines multiple photos captured at various exposure levels 
to counterbalance digital cameras' limited dynamic range. This research presents a 
technique for automatically determining optimal exposure settings for smartphone 
images, enabling the construction of a mobile HDR-capable camera system. The 
proposed method employs a three-step approach to analyze the relationship between 
exposure settings, image histogram data, and perceived visual noise. Initially, 
the optimal exposure settings are determined in relation to the image's visual 
noise. Next, a noise metric is developed to quantify visual noise from histogram 
data. Finally, the technique is refined to accommodate varying scene brightness 
levels. The proposed system was tested on 20 different outdoor scenes and 20 
indoor scenes in urban settings, resulting in a 2.5 dB gain in HDR image quality 
compared to standard HDR techniques. The system's effectiveness was found to be 
less consistent in low-light conditions. The research demonstrates the feasibility 
of a mobile HDR camera system using a single camera. The proposed technique 
exhibits improved performance when compared to existing methods, particularly in 
brightly lit scenes. The system's source code is available online. The impact of 
the proposed technique on various image quality assessment algorithms is also 
examined. The research's findings contribute to the development of more advanced 
HDR algorithms and image quality assessment methods. The system's code has been 
hosted on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/aliakbarian/MobileHDR. The

Causal deep learning, an emerging field that applies causal analysis to
neural networks, has shown significant promise in improving predictions and
inference. However, the scarcity of available methods and limited understanding
of their advantages and disadvantages hinders researchers and practitioners.
This tutorial aims to bridge this gap by presenting three key aspects of
causal deep learning: identifying causal relationships within neural networks using
learning equations, pinpointing the sources of adversarial vulnerabilities,
and using causal analysis to prevent them from occurring. Specifically, we will
introduce SCAD, a method for reconstructing neural network learning equations and
its applications in both transfer learning and adversarial attacks. Furthermore,
we will delve into the underlying mechanisms of adversarial attacks and present
two approaches based on the Backdoor Detection Tool and SCAD, illustrating
how to locate and remove backdoors from neural networks. Through this tutorial,
we hope to provide a comprehensive introduction to causal deep learning and its
various applications, paving the way for further research in this exciting
field. Code for this tutorial can be found in the following repository: https://github.com/chen310/CDL-Tutorial. Keywords: Causal Deep Learning, Neural Networks, Adversarial Attacks, Transfer Learning, Backdoor Detection. Code link: https://github.com/chen310/CDL-Tutorial. Relevant to wide-ranging challenges, reinforcement learning solutions often struggle with sudden changes in task environments. Our investigation focuses on a specific aspect of this difficulty, examining how it affects a critical task: detecting and removing adverse data. We define "adverse data" as labeled information that is incorrect and could be detrimental to machine learning, given its potential to steer a model towards biased and inaccurate predictions. Our primary objective is to develop a protocol for identifying and removing such harmful information from a dataset using only the data itself, without relying on external guidance. We introduce an initial model that, due to its limitations, frequently produces conflicting outcomes when attempting to distinguish between adverse and beneficial data. To address this issue, we develop two complementary RL-based detection methods. The first method, AdverseDataDiscoverer, learns to identify adverse data by associating it with a model's prediction errors and penalizing the model for such associations. The second method, AdverseDataCorrector, trains a model to remove adverse data by guiding it towards producing more accurate predictions and penalizing the model for producing associated predictions. Our experiments demonstrate that both detection approaches succeed in removing adverse data, with AdverseDataDiscoverer excelling in identifying a larger portion of adverse data and AdverseDataCorrector performing better in removing a larger quantity of adverse data. Furthermore, our findings reveal that both methods can effectively integrate prior knowledge and that AdverseDataDiscoverer is highly effective in removing a significant portion of adverse data even in dynamic and open-world settings. Our research provides a starting point for exploring the challenges associated with detecting and removing adverse data within machine learning models, as well as the potential risks and benefits of incorporating external guidance in this process. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhongyuan-liu/AdverseDataDiscovery. Our investigation highlights the difficulties that machine learning models face when encountering adverse data and emphasizes the significance of further research into the design of robust models capable of distinguishing between beneficial and adverse data without external guidance. Our findings also underscore the value of exploring detection and removal strategies that leverage the internal knowledge of machine learning models themselves. Our research is relevant to a range of applications, including, but not limited to, removing biased data from historical employment records, eliminating incorrect training data in online machine learning, and removing adverse data from Wikipedia. Understanding business processes relies on process discovery methods, analyzing data trails to reveal underlying processes. As processes evolve over time, their corresponding models must adapt, otherwise they may inaccurately predict future behaviors. This paper focuses on identifying changes to a dynamic process, using partial data from a specific moment, and explores how to modify existing models to match this partial data, assessing their validity and potential improvements. A framework is established to identify altered activities, their timing, and reasons, and an algorithm is developed to map these changes to a process model, refining it to better fit the observed data. This approach is demonstrated through real-world examples and evaluated using real process data, showing that even with limited data, processes can be accurately modified, and that this approach outperforms existing methods in evaluating and refining process models dynamically. This research is relevant to various domains, including, but not limited to, healthcare, finance, and manufacturing, where process changes are common and valuable, and can be applied to both constrained and prioritized processes. A theoretical analysis and empirical studies show that this approach can effectively manage process changes, even with minimal available data. This work lays the groundwork for further research into how to manage process changes, and highlights the significance of considering process dynamics when designing data mining methods, and evaluating process models. This study aims to advance the sentiment analysis method without labeled data by integrating multiple auxiliary tasks and utilizes a specially designed multi-task deep neural network to conduct the analysis. Initially, a task set is established based on available labeled data and resources, then the network is trained to accomplish these tasks for the target domain. Next, auxiliary tasks are identified to be incorporated into the set, with the goal of reducing overfitting when performing the primary tasks on the unlabeled data for the domain. Three methods are then proposed to integrate these tasks, with the network being trained on all available data after the set is finalized. The network is then trained on the primary tasks using either positive or unlabeled data for the domain. A wide range of experiments are conducted to evaluate the proposed method, with the results showing that it outperforms the current state-of-the-art approaches in multiple scenarios. Furthermore, the proposed method is found to be effective even when the tasks are highly related, which is often the case in many applications. In addition, the proposed method is applied to a real-world scenario, with the results indicating that it can be used to reduce the amount of labeled data required for a specific domain by as much as three orders of magnitude. The classical universal bundle functor that maps a simplicial group to the simplicial group of functions from the standard simplicial interval to the group in question has been a fundamental concept in algebraic topology. This functor can be generalized to a wide range of simplicial algebras, including groups, rings, and lattices, and it has been observed that it extends to a natural transformation that maps a simplicial algebra to the image of the simplicial standard interval under the universal bundle functor, but with the simplicial structure lost. This loss of structure can be rectified by constructing a new simplicial structure on the image of the standard simplicial interval, which we call the ``thin" simplicial structure. This construction is particularly significant for groups, as it results in a group whose homotopy type is equivalent to the original group but with a simpler simplicial structure. As a result, the universal bundle functor can be naturally extended to a functor that maps a simplicial group to the group of functions from the standard simplicial interval to the original group, with the simplicial structure on the latter group modified to the "thin" structure. This extension enables the development of a more sophisticated model for the universal bundle functor based on the combinatorial properties of the standard simplicial interval, which in turn provides a more in-depth understanding of the fundamental properties of this functor. This knowledge can be applied to various applications, including the study of crossed complexes and their relationship to the fundamental groupoid of a space. This approach also offers insights into the properties of homotopy groups and the connections between them and the groups of the "thin" simplicial groups associated with a given space. This association gives rise to a functor from the fundamental groupoid of a space to the family of "thin" simplicial groups associated with it, which in turn leads to a connection between the homotopy groups of a space and the groups of the "thin" simplicial groups associated with it. This connection, in turn, enables the development of a model for the reduced conjugacy classes of a group, which can be used to study the relationship between a group and its homotopy groups. This relationship is particularly significant for fundamental groups of finite-dimensional manifolds, which are characterized by having trivial reduced conjugacy classes. We investigated the interplay between dark matter and baryonic matter in massive galaxies with irregular stellar disks using the power spectrum analysis of stellar and gas distributions. By examining the power spectra of 13 such galaxies at different redshifts, we found a consistent pattern where the power spectra of their stellar and gas distributions exhibit a break point shifting towards lower wave numbers as time progresses. This phenomenon can be attributed to the suppression of star formation in these galaxies' outer regions. Furthermore, by linking the power spectra of their mass and distribution to their assembly histories, we discovered that the missing mass in dark matter halos is compensated by an increase in the mass of baryonic matter within the inner region of the halo, while the outer region experiences a decline in mass density due to the inhibited star formation and subsequent ejection of stars and gas. Consequently, these galaxies' evolution are locked in a cycle of mass redistribution, with the inner region consuming the outer region, and the resulting morphology is a signature of this interplay. The rapid dissemination of information through social media poses a significant threat to public safety, as it can spread false information about critical events before genuine details become available. Traditional detection methods, which rely on large amounts of labeled data and specific categories of misinformation, struggle to effectively tackle the problem of real-time fake news detection for emerging events. To address this challenge, we propose a novel framework called EventFakeNet that utilizes a combination of transfer learning and a multi-task approach to leverage the information available during such events. Specifically, our framework leverages the semantic meaning of event-related keywords to generate an initial set of fake news examples, which it then uses to train a multi-task CNN-DNN model. The model is designed to distinguish between genuine and fabricated news while simultaneously identifying the most relevant information that characterizes the event in question. We evaluated our framework on a newly created dataset consisting of 1,500 real-world news articles and 10 distinct events, and the results showed that it outperforms existing detection methods while maintaining high efficiency. Moreover, our analysis revealed that the integration of semantic information enhances the detection accuracy by facilitating the creation of high-quality negative examples and the incorporation of crucial event-related details. To enhance understanding of these interactions, researchers are examining the behavior of silicon crystals with precisely located phosphorus dopants. By utilizing terahertz spectroscopy, scientists have discovered a way to directly observe the quantum fluctuations of electric fields within these crystals. A recent breakthrough has seen the development of a technique to precisely manipulate the position of individual dopants to create arrays of isolated, doped silicon sites. Building upon this advancement, a study has been conducted that investigates the behavior of a large, isolated silicon crystal lattice's quantum fluctuations through terahertz spectroscopy, revealing a previously unknown aspect of its physical response. The findings of this research reveal that the physical response of a silicon crystal to terahertz radiation is influenced by both the Coulomb interaction with dopants and the quantum nature of its own electrons. A theoretical model has been created to interpret the data and demonstrates that the terahertz response of a silicon crystal is characterized by an unusual frequency range that is determined by the quantum fluctuations of its own electrons. This range can be adjusted by modifying the distance between silicon atoms through either isotopic substitution or thermal expansion. The results of this research have significant implications for the development of quantum computers that rely on silicon crystals with precise dopants, as they suggest that the quantum nature of the electrons within the crystal itself could pose a challenge for maintaining quantum coherence over extended periods. The discovery of this controllable aspect of terahertz radiation could drive advancements in fields like materials science and quantum physics. Complex systems with interacting components are ubiquitous in physics, biology, and engineering. These systems often follow nonlinear dynamics, and understanding their behavior is crucial for predicting and controlling their evolution. By casting the dynamics as a nonlinear grid-based neural network, we developed a method to efficiently train a linear graph neural network to match the nonlinear dynamics at multiple resolution levels. This approach ensures that the network's scaling properties are maintained across resolutions, facilitating the analysis of scaling behavior and allowing for the identification of critical points. We applied this technique to study the dynamics of dimer models, self-consistent field theories, and the Ising model on a lattice, and demonstrated that it accurately captures the dynamics of these systems even at low resolutions. Furthermore, we found that the network's scaling properties align with established critical exponents in the Ising model, and that it can pinpoint the location of phase transitions within a small resolution error. This method provides a versatile tool for investigating the dynamics of complex systems and uncovering the characteristics of phase transitions. We have made our code publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhengyiwang/gnn_dynamics. As an example of its utility, we used this method to explore the dynamics of a random field Ising model and discovered a first-order phase transition at f=1, which had previously been hypothesized but not empirically confirmed. This finding is supported by the scaling behavior of the network, and we have released the associated data on FigShare at https://doi.org/10.6088/202304301548. We anticipate that this approach will be valuable for analyzing a wide range of complex systems and their nonlinear dynamics. Dimensionality reduction in high-dimensional data is effectively managed by a technique called feature extraction. Self-supervised learning, in particular contrastive learning, has gained popularity in this area due to the lack of labeled data. A novel method called Semi-Supervised Multi-Sample Contrastive Network (SSMCN) is presented in this paper, which applies contrastive learning to feature extraction. Unlike existing contrastive learning techniques that compare individual samples, SSMCN compares the intrinsic similarity between multiple distribution sets, resulting in a robust general-purpose feature extractor. The distinction of SSMCN from other methods lies in its capacity to compare multiple data points, allowing it to be utilized for both supervised and unsupervised learning problems. Experimental results demonstrate that SSMCN outperforms multiple baselines in classification tasks for several datasets, and its ability to compare multiple data sets makes it suitable for clustering problems as well. Furthermore, SSMCN's performance is found to be comparable to supervised learning in many instances. The code of SSMCN is available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/zhengzheng-1998/SSMCN.

Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on numerous language tasks. However, there's still room for improvement when processing structured information, particularly knowledge encoded in graphs. We investigate the potential benefits of incorporating knowledge graphs into LLMs and propose a method to leverage LLMs as neural pattern matching machines. Our approach maps knowledge graph triples to LLM embeddings, enabling the model to recognize structured relationships and demonstrate its effectiveness in several structured language understanding tasks. Our results show that incorporating knowledge graphs through this method surpasses traditional approaches, including using natural language sentences, and provides a scalable solution by utilizing pre-trained LLMs as the base model. Moreover, our study reveals the impact of different relation matching strategies on performance and identifies key factors influencing the effectiveness of structured knowledge, including graph size, relation matching methods, and LLM types. Our code and models are available at https://github.com/ghru/structured-lm.

To address this issue, we developed a method for efficiently achieving high-quality anti-aliasing in vector maps under various rendering scales and orientations. By examining various rendering techniques and anti-aliasing methods, we identified a novel approach that leverages the characteristics of Bezier curves to provide a precise anti-aliased rendering effect. Furthermore, we optimized this technique for different rendering scales and orientations in two operations: first, determining the optimal anti-aliasing strategy based on the curvature of the map, and second, developing an algorithm to detect and handle line crossings that occur during high-scale rendering. Our approach was tested on a range of vector maps and demonstrated significant improvements in visual quality and reduced computational overhead in comparison to existing solutions. To enhance the modeling of long sequences in the time domain for speech separation, a dual-path RNN was previously proposed, which combines a short-term memory network with a long-term RNN. However, the performance of this model can be limited by its reliance on manually set hyperparameters to balance the contributions of short- and long-term components. Building upon this dual-path RNN model, we present a novel, self-adaptive time-domain speech separation architecture that leverages dual-path RNNs and neural network dynamics to capture both short- and long-term patterns in speech. The proposed model's unique design enables the automatic identification of time frames governed by either the short- or long-term RNN components, allowing it to adapt to a wide range of input lengths without the need for hyperparameter tuning. Experimental evaluations conducted on the Wall Street Journal dataset demonstrate the proposed model's capability to efficiently handle varying sequence lengths and its superior speech separation performance relative to competing techniques. The model's versatility and superior performance are further highlighted by the success of a continuous speech separation task, where the model is trained on short utterances and applied to separate continuous speech. The results of this experiment show that the model achieves comparable separation performance to a batch-based approach, despite being trained on significantly shorter data samples. The model's code is available at this link: https://github.com/zhengzhengyjy/SAD-TDSS.

Recent advancements in multi-fluid models aim to enhance the simulation of atmospheric convection within weather and climate simulations. By breaking down a single, unified fluid into distinct, interacting fluid components, these models better capture the behavior of turbulent, multi-phase atmospheric phenomena, such as cumulus convection and atmospheric waves. In this study, we integrated a multi-fluid model into the Met Office Unified Model and evaluated its performance in a high-altitude region with significant convection. Our analysis focused on Mount Everest and the surrounding area during the pre-monsoon season. We analyzed the model's ability to simulate temperature, humidity, and wind patterns using in-situ measurements from the 2005 GOring III expedition. Our findings indicate that the multi-fluid model successfully replicates the temperature and humidity gradients observed at high elevations and accurately captures the behavior of atmospheric waves. However, it also introduces an error in the simulation of lower atmospheric temperature and humidity levels. Our research demonstrates the multi-fluid model's capacity to capture high-altitude temperature inversions and the associated atmospheric wave patterns, and we believe its application could be beneficial for weather and climate simulations in mountainous regions. In these environments, the model offers improved performance over traditional single-fluid models, particularly when simulating the behavior of atmospheric waves and temperature inversions at high elevations. Our study also highlights the model's limitations in simulating turbulence and mass flux processes, which are critical components of convection in lower altitude regions. As a result, we recommend the multi-fluid model be used in conjunction with a high-resolution, single-fluid model in areas with intense convection, such as tropical regions. In these regions, the model may struggle to capture the mass flux processes and turbulence characteristic of deep convection, and it may require significant grid resolution improvements. Reconstructing a quantum state of continuous-variable systems like the radiation field is highly challenging due to the infinite number of degrees of freedom. Multiple approaches to obtaining the Wigner function from an optical tomogram of a light state have been proposed, each with its limitations and requirements for the state preparation and measurement processes. We demonstrate that the positive Wigner function of an arbitrary two-mode state can be determined from its optical tomogram, regardless of the underlying dynamics. This result applies to both discrete and continuous measurements of any light field and provides a universal method for extracting the Wigner function from the optical tomogram of a single-mode state in certain scenarios. Our findings are experimentally verified using a two-mode Squeezed Light Source, offering a valuable step towards accurate reconstruction of continuous-variable quantum states via optical tomography. We also discuss the extension of our approach to qudipartite systems, leading to a discussion on the Heisenberg limit in multi-mode settings. 360-degree streaming videos can significantly enhance the virtual tourism experience by allowing users to freely navigate immersive, panoramic scenes. However, the complexity of these videos makes them challenging to stream over the internet. To address this issue, a proposed 360-degree video streaming framework pre-renders videos on smart glasses devices, leveraging their built-in accelerators to speed up playback efficiency. The framework optimizes video rendering based on user movement data and the limited battery power of portable devices. To facilitate seamless streaming, it develops a real-time streaming and synchronization system that pre-renders and streams 360-degree videos at 30 frames per second on various devices, meeting the requirements of both streaming and rendering tasks while minimizing power consumption. Experimental results show that the proposed framework achieves higher rendering efficiency and better visual effects than existing methods. Moreover, it offers a user-friendly and immersive virtual tourism experience that can be expanded to other portable, low-power devices. Tensor network methods have become a versatile toolbox for solving a wide range of computational problems in physics, stemming from their ability to fuse local degrees of freedom to achieve a balance between conflicting requirements in modeling critical phenomena, both in real and imaginary time. A critical aspect of these methods is identifying suitable bond dimension, which can be achieved through various algorithms such as the Algebraic Distance Algorithm, the Power Algorithm, and the Newton-Successive Algorithm. However, these methods are generally based on numerical approximations and may yield unstable or biased outcomes. In contrast, the Algebraic Distance Algorithm, which utilizes a direct and efficient approach to find the nearest left/right anti-symmetric matrix within a given set, has shown promise in maintaining the genuine properties of the target tensor. In this work, we introduce a novel variant of the Algebraic Distance Algorithm, the ADAlight algorithm, which specifically targets anti-symmetric matrices with a non-negative eigenvalue spectrum. The resulting algorithm maintains the lightness constraint while minimizing the distance between the desired tensor and the proposed solution, and is applicable to a broad spectrum of tensor network scenarios. Our variant, which includes a modified version of the Algebraic Distance Algorithm, is accompanied by a comprehensive theoretical analysis of its performance, and is demonstrated to converge to an optimal solution in the space of anti-symmetric matrices with non-negative eigenvalues. Through a series of numerical examples and simulations, we show that the ADAlight algorithm outperforms its competitors in terms of precision and efficiency in finding the optimal solution. The resulting algorithm has been implemented in a user-friendly format for easy access and utilization by the wider community. The associated code can be found at https://github.com/zhenghenghanhan/ADAlight. The theoretical underpinnings and the algorithm's performance are thoroughly examined in the following sections. The method's applicability is also highlighted through concrete numerical examples. The code for the ADAlight algorithm is available at https://github.com/zhenghenghanhan/ADAlight. The code is written in Python 3.9 and utilizes the TensorFlow 2.4.1 framework. The associated documentation can be found at https://adalight.readthedocs.io/. We develop a decoupling theory for a diverse range of high-order smooth surfaces in three-dimensional space without planar components. Our approach can also handle surfaces described by non-uniform polynomial equations. By examining these surfaces, we create an opportunity to adapt and expand the concept of linear decoupling, incorporating a combination of Taylor series analysis and the development of a library of reference surfaces to facilitate approximation and decoupling purposes. Ultimately, our work provides a foundation for exploring and generalizing our findings to other types of surfaces. As additional contributions, we derive and study specific surface models, analyze their properties and behavior, and demonstrate the applicability of our methods through numerical examples. Additionally, we outline potential future directions for our research. As a supplementary resource, we have made available an interactive tool, known as the Decoupling Surface Explorer, which allows users to dynamically explore and visualize various surfaces and related decoupling transformations within a three-dimensional space. This interactive tool is accessible online. As a related but distinct project, we have also developed an earlier decoupling theory tailored to a subset of surfaces, which we have previously described in a separate research paper. As an illustration of our method's versatility, we have applied and adapted this earlier theory to create a novel acoustic metamaterial design, which can be found in the accompanying paper titled "A Nonplanar Acoustic Metamaterial Based on a Decoupling Surface" by Y. Zhang, Y. Chen, and J. Li. Notably, this research has been inspired by and builds upon the concepts presented in the aforementioned paper by Zhang et al. which was published in the journal Physical Review Applied in 2021. In that earlier work, a fundamental decoupling surface theory was developed specifically for linear acoustic applications and demonstrated the creation of a nonplanar acoustic metamaterial using a decoupling surface, but it was limited to surfaces defined by quadratic polynomial equations. In contrast, the current research expands upon that foundation by generalizing the decoupling surface concept to include higher-order polynomial surfaces, thus significantly broadening its applicability. As a result, this generalized decoupling surface model now offers the flexibility to design acoustic metamaterials using a wide range of surface shapes, including those described by both uniform and non-uniform polynomial equations. As an added feature, we have made available an online tool, known as the Decoupling Surface Generator, which allows users to generate and visualize these surfaces, along with the associated decoupling transformations, in three-dimensional space. The impact of infrared renormalons in the color dipole gluon distribution's variance is being quantified, and calculations demonstrate how non-linear small-x saturation impacts shift the Borel plane's initial IR pole from $b=-1$ to $b=-3$. As a result, we find that the moment of the gluon distribution, calculated to four-loop order, has a larger negative pole than expected based on linearized Borel resummation. Furthermore, the variance of the dipole gluon distribution's scattering off a proton at infrared loop depth requires the inclusion of a $(-4)$ branch cut in the Borel plane. The cut's impact is comparable to that of higher-loop corrections from the hard part of the scattering process. The issue of IR renormalons in the gluon distribution's variance also affects the distribution's average and impacts the Froissart bound on deep inelastic scattering cross-sections. The influence of these results on the Froissart bound is being examined, and we find that the bound remains unaffected. The same approach can be applied to other gluon distributions constructed from the dipole gluon distribution. The method presented in this research can be used to calculate the impact of IR renormalons on other deep inelastic scattering processes. Deep neural networks experience significant performance improvements when trained using multiple GPUs, but the resulting benefits can be fleeting if knowledge distillation is not effectively utilized. To address this challenge, we present GDF, a novel knowledge distillation method that facilitates efficient knowledge transfer between large and small models during parallel training. Unlike conventional knowledge distillation approaches that rely on reconstruction of intermediate layer representations, GDF directly manipulates soft labels to enhance model performance. Theoretical and empirical evidence demonstrate that soft labels serve as control variables for model parameters, allowing us to develop a general framework for knowledge distillation. Furthermore, we introduce an optimization strategy based on the theoretical framework, which leverages the smoothness regularization of soft labels to improve model performance. Experimental evaluations using ResNet50 and EfficientNet demonstrate that GDF achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art knowledge distillation methods while significantly reducing computational costs. Additionally, our approach can be applied to various knowledge distillation scenarios, yielding consistent performance gains. The code for GDF is available at https://github.com/zhengyong-yu/GDF.

Constructing the lattice of submodules of a given module is generally a complicated task. However, for certain modules with specific properties, specifically direct products and direct sums of modules, algorithms exist that efficiently construct their lattice of submodules by breaking them down into components and using previously established methods for simple modules. This research extends those capabilities to modules that are components of direct products and sums, mapping the lattice of their submodules based on the lattices of the corresponding component modules. A key step in achieving this mapping involves identifying and analyzing the "join irreducible" submodules of the component modules. Join irreducible submodules are then utilized as building blocks to construct the lattice of submodules of the original module. As a result, this work provides a method for constructing the lattice of submodules of modules that are components of direct products and sums, offering implications for understanding the structural relationships within these modules. Furthermore, this research can be applied to modules associated with the lattice of order-ideals of certain posets, specifically join trees and free sequences, which were previously unstudied entities in the literature. This research also introduces the concept of free sequences as a module-theoretic analogue of free sequences in poset theory. It demonstrates that the lattice of order-ideals of a free sequence is isomorphic to the lattice of submodules of a specific module, providing a theoretical framework that can be utilized to investigate the properties of these lattices. Additionally, this framework enables the creation of test cases for examining the validity of conjectures related to these lattices. As a result, this research contributes to the understanding of module-related structures and facilitates the testing of existing conjectures about the lattice of order-ideals of free sequences and join trees. It also lays the groundwork for exploring modules associated with other poset structures. As a related finding, this research uncovers that the poset structure of join trees can be recovered from the lattice of order-ideals of a free sequence that is derived from the same set of elements. Consequently, this research reveals that the poset structure of series-parallel posets is equivalent to the join tree structure, which was an unknown relationship in the literature. As a result, this research provides a module-theoretic interpretation of series-parallel posets, offering a new perspective on their characteristics. It also demonstrates that the width of a join tree is equivalent to the width of the associated module, whereas the width of a free sequence is equivalent to the uniform width of the associated module. Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, a novel approach is presented that utilizes performance feedback from a second-agent relative, rather than demonstrations, to train a reinforcement learning agent. We introduce a new policy optimization method called Contrastive Policy Optimization (CPO), which incorporates contrastive learning to train the agent based on the relative feedback. CPO's effectiveness is demonstrated through two agent-relative learning scenarios: one with a fixed reward function and the other with an unknown, evolving rewards structure. The proposed approach is shown to achieve superior performance compared to standard policy optimization, and the parameters of CPO can be tuned to balance efficiency in dynamic environments. The underlying technique of using an agent relative for feedback can be applied to various learning settings, and we term this general paradigm Relative Learning. The resulting CPO framework and Relative Learning concept are expected to contribute to the development of efficient learning methods in complex and dynamic environments. A novel metric function is proposed for decoding polarization-adjusted convolutional (PAC) codes, resulting in a significant improvement in their error-correction performance. This optimal decoding metric prioritizes the minimization of bit errors in the most reliably transmitted bits, thereby focusing on the most critical errors. The modified metric is specifically designed to account for the channel's reliability information, which is readily available in quasi-static channels. As a convolutional code, PAC codes maintain a minimum distance of at least 1, and as such, their error-correction performance is comparable to that of low-density parity-check convolutional codes under ideal decoding conditions. However, with the proposed optimal metric, PAC codes exhibit a noticeable improvement in bit error rates at low SNRs, demonstrating the potential benefits of this decoding strategy. The optimal metric can be implemented using a stack or branch-and-bound decoder. A simulated example is provided to illustrate the effectiveness of this metric in reducing bit errors in a quasi-static AWGN channel using 64-ary PSK modulation. The results also highlight the trade-offs between code memory and the required SNR for a certain error rate, and demonstrate the applicability of this decoding strategy to other types of polar codes. The optimal metric can be viewed as a form of list decoding, where the list size is limited to one, and its implementation is found to offer a lower decoding complexity than traditional list decoding methods. The associated increase in required SNR is, however, relatively small, and the error-correction performance improvement is more substantial. The impact of the metric on the decoding process is also examined, and the associated complexity is found to scale linearly with the memory of the code. The optimal metric function can be viewed as a form of weighted soft-decision decoding, where the weights reflect the reliability of the channel, and its performance is found to approach that of ideal decoding as the SNR increases. The associated gap in bit error rates is found to decrease with increasing code memory, and the required SNR for a certain error rate is found to scale linearly with the memory of the code. The performance of this decoding strategy is compared to that of other decoding methods for PAC codes, including a conventional soft-decision decoder, a stack decoder, and a list decoder, and its performance is found to approach that of ideal decoding more closely than these methods in the low-SNR regime. The study of open quantum systems under periodic driving forces is highly relevant to quantum thermalization, as it allows for the investigation of non-equilibrium steady states in these systems. Recent research has revealed that driven open quantum systems with access to a quantum bath can achieve periodic steady states, even when there are dissipation barriers to reach thermal equilibrium with their surroundings. This work focuses on discrete time-driven scenarios and demonstrates that periodic driving can lead to state entanglement enhancement in multi-partite systems, potentially serving as a resource for quantum computation. A continuous time-driven model is also presented, along with a proposal for experimental implementation using laser cooling of ions in an optical trap. This paper explores the optimization challenges in multi-agent systems that involve agents behaving maliciously, which leads to a misdirection away from optimal solutions through the spread of false information and significant communication costs. To address this issue, we develop a distributed optimization algorithm based on gradient updates, where trustworthy agents share quantized data with each other. This is further illustrated through numerical experiments presented in the study. Our findings can be applied to a range of applications, including those mentioned above, and provide a framework for designing robust distributed optimization systems in the presence of malicious agents. Building upon this foundation, he presented two specific problems concerning the embedding of spaces with angle functions into the structure of Euclidean spaces. Over time, researchers have tackled these problems, yet they remain largely unsolved. This paper aims to contribute new insights by exploring the relationship between spaces with angle functions and Euclidean spaces, specifically within the context of isometric embeddings in the presence of a third element. It demonstrates that such an element can be used as a point of reference to establish a correspondence between the spaces with angle functions and Euclidean spaces of higher dimensions, thereby affirmatively answering both of Menger's problems. Additionally, this paper presents a novel characterization of spaces with angle functions that provides a more refined understanding of their geometric properties. Futhermore, it reveals that certain configurations, initially considered as special cases, actually represent general conditions applicable to spaces with angle functions. This newfound insight is then applied to investigate specific types of spaces with angle functions, including those with angular distances that are congruent to linear functions, and offers a more general framework for studying the geometric properties of these spaces. This research was inspired by the work of mathematician B. Wegener, who previously explored spaces with angle functions but was limited to examining the properties of specific dimensions. In contrast, the discoveries presented in this paper are dimensionally agnostic. This study was also motivated by the investigation of certain types of spaces with angle functions, specifically those with angular distances defined by Euclidean metrics in Euclidean spaces of higher dimensions, and the newly introduced concept of hyperbolic spaces with angle functions. This paper demonstrates that the angular distances in Euclidean spaces of n dimensions can be matched to linear functions, and it also uncovers the distinctive properties of spaces with angle functions in Euclidean spaces of n-dimensional hyperbolic spaces. This research was further expanded in a related study that explored the connection between spaces with angle functions and the concept of visibility, and revealed that certain types of spaces with angle functions are visible, and that the visibility of these spaces is directly linked to their dimension. This discovery led to the development of a new dimensionality criterion that can be applied to any space with angle functions. Developing neural text generation models via Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) remains a challenging task due to the slow convergence of the generator network. To address this issue, we propose a novel training method that utilizes a multi-agent framework to train multiple, distinct generator networks, which operate on the same data distribution space but produce unique, independent text samples. We show that the generator networks can be trained at a faster rate and with improved stability, compared to traditional adversarial training methods. Furthermore, we introduce a Multi-Agent GAN (MAGAN) model that combines multiple generator networks into a single, advanced model, resulting in improved performance. Experimental evaluations using text generation tasks demonstrate the effectiveness and superiority of our proposed method. We have released the code and models associated with this research.

The concept of interstellar panspermia, which suggests life could be transported from one planetary system to another, is a captivating idea, but it's difficult to verify through observations of our own solar system. A possible indicator of interstellar panspermia is the presence of life-related organic compounds that are more abundant in molecular clouds than in local space, which could be achieved through the transportation of these compounds from the solar system. However, estimating the quantity of these compounds in molecular clouds is challenging due to their widespread contamination with organics originating from the solar system. A new study suggests that certain molecular clouds may contain fewer local contaminants than previously thought, which could make the detection of more abundant extraterrestrial organics possible. By examining the composition of gas and dust in the molecular cloud complex called the Local Bubble, researchers found that it is likely enriched with high-molecular-weight organic compounds of interstellar origin. If this finding is confirmed, it could provide evidence for the transportation of life-related compounds and support the interstellar panspermia hypothesis. Moreover, the discovery of these compounds within the Local Bubble could also contribute to a better understanding of the distribution and evolution of organic matter within our solar system. If the results are validated, they could have implications for the search for life beyond Earth, suggesting that the availability of life-related compounds in molecular clouds may be more accessible than previously thought. This study's findings are also relevant to the study of comets, which are known to harbor a wide range of organic compounds, and could provide insights into the origins of these compounds within comets. If the Local Bubble is found to be a reservoir of cometary material, it could help explain the diversity of organic compounds found in comets. This research also sheds light on the potential sources of life-related compounds found in meteorites, which could be linked to the transportation of these compounds from molecular clouds to planetary bodies. This study's results are based on an analysis of the distribution of gas and dust within the Local Bubble, which was obtained through a combination of satellite data and ground-based observations. This analysis revealed that the compounds in the Local Bubble are not locally produced, but rather are made up of a mixture of pre-existing materials that have been preserved over millions of years. This preservation of compounds over such a long period is consistent with the low rate of destruction of these compounds in low-density environments. This study's findings have implications for our understanding of the distribution and evolution of organic matter within our solar system, and could contribute to a better comprehension of the origins of life-related compounds

Understanding animal habitat preferences is crucial for wildlife research and conservation, and is often achieved by analyzing locations previously used by animals. We developed a method that uses a Gaussian process to model the expected utility of using different locations, and applied it to a study of black bears in North America. This approach also allowed us to identify the most preferred locations and predict the utility of using new locations. In contrast to traditional methods, our approach can account for the trade-offs animals make when using multiple resources, and can be used with small samples of used locations. We also introduced a method to account for the spatial autocorrelation often present in animal locations, and found that it significantly improved the accuracy of our results. We believe this approach has broad applications in studying the habitats and resource use of animals.

The analysis of multilayer networks has been utilized to model various dynamic systems, offering a more precise representation than single-layer networks, albeit at the cost of increased analytical complexity. To overcome this challenge, we present a method for examining the time-evolving patterns of node connections within multilayer networks by applying a non-parametric degree distribution approach. This approach allows us to investigate the changes in network structure over time, comparing them to a set of time-averaged reference networks, and to compare the dynamics of multilayer networks to those of single-layer networks. As a specific application, we utilize this approach to analyze the temporal evolution of a co-authorship network among researchers at the Santa Fe Complex Systems Summer School. Notably, our findings reveal distinct single-layer networks within this multilayer network, which we confirm through additional data sources and research. By leveraging this multilayer network model, we uncover its underlying dynamics and compare them to those of single-layer networks, revealing that they adhere to similar power-law distributions but exhibit different scaling properties along their longitudinal dimensions. Our research demonstrates that multilayer networks can effectively capture the complex evolution of dynamic systems, especially those influenced by time-varying connections, and provide valuable insights into their internal dynamics. Our approach is versatile and can be adapted for the analysis of other multilayer networks exhibiting non-stationary behavior. Our approach takes a property to be tested as input and provides a theoretically grounded, two-step testing procedure to verify the property. First, we perform a preliminary check to ensure the property in question is valid for a program's specified semantics. If this check succeeds, we can then employ a testing strategy that prioritizes inputs leading to the property's counterfactuals – in other words, the situations in which the property would be violated. Our method guarantees that, through a finite set of counterexample-driven tests, we can conclusively establish the property's validity or obtain a counterexample to demonstrate the property's falsehood. Our approach is underpinned by novel theoretical verifications of key testing-related properties, and we also provide empirical data highlighting the practical effectiveness of our integrated verification and testing framework. In particular, our results indicate that a significant portion of properties associated with real-world programs can be efficiently validated or invalidated through our testing methodology. The anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials, a phenomenon that generates voltage perpendicular to current flow and magnetization, has been studied extensively. The largest anomalous Hall response found to date has been in the compound Ir2(III)(Si2S5) Cl2, with a coefficient of around 4.7 x 10^-3 Ohm cm per unit of magnetic moment. Researchers have now surpassed this record with the discovery of Ir2(IV)(Si2S5) Cl2, yielding an even greater response of approximately 6.1 x 10^-3 Ohm cm per unit of magnetic moment. The enhanced effect in this compound is attributed to the unique electronic structure resulting from the presence of Ir(IV) ions. The large anomalous Hall response in this material may lead to breakthroughs in the development of compact, energy-efficient devices. The record has been broken in the class of transition metal compounds with chalcogenide thiophosphate halides, and the study of this material's electronic and magnetic properties is ongoing. The anomalous Hall effect in this material is found to be stable over a broad temperature range and is accompanied by an unusual magnetic behavior. The discovery of this material has been confirmed through multiple techniques including X-ray diffraction, X-ray absorption spectroscopy, and scanning tunneling microscopy. The findings of this study are expected to inspire further research into the anomalous Hall effect in other transition metal compounds with chalcogenide thiophosphate halides. The material's unique properties make it an ideal candidate for the study of the anomalous Nernst effect and the anomalous spin rotation, and it may also be suitable for applications in spin-based information storage and magnetoresistive sensors. The study of this material has been published in the journal Nature Materials. The integration of artificial intelligence in materials research leverages computational power to analyze vast amounts of data, leading to a paradigm shift in scientific inquiry. Machine learning techniques, which analyze complex relationships and enable predictions, are being applied to a wide range of materials properties and behavior. In this review, we examine the use of machine learning in materials physics through a data-driven approach, exploring how it can be both a powerful tool and a method of last resort. We begin by exploring how machine learning is a natural fit for materials research, then delve into specific examples of its application, including materials discovery, phase transitions, and materials degradation. We also discuss the challenges faced when combining machine learning and materials research, including the need for open data and accessible code. Finally, we outline potential future directions for this field of research. By taking a data-driven approach, we provide an analysis of the materials research published in the journal Physical Review Materials over the past five years, highlighting the most commonly studied materials, research methods, and machine learning techniques used within the field. We also examine the relationship between machine learning and materials research through a network theory perspective, revealing the interconnectedness of the field's research components. We conclude by emphasizing the importance of open data and accessible code in materials research, and the need for machine learning to be viewed as an integral part of the scientific method. We make our analysis and methodology available to the public through an online companion, which can be accessed at this link: https://www.prm.org/insights/machine-learning-materials-research. We hope this review and our accompanying analysis will serve as a resource for researchers within the field, and provide a foundation for future studies on machine learning in materials physics. We also invite readers to contribute to our ongoing research by sharing their own data and research with us. We believe that through the open sharing of data and research, we can accelerate the discovery of new materials and the advancement of materials research as a whole. We are committed to making our own research data openly available, and we encourage other researchers to follow the same principles. We hope that our review and our accompanying analysis will contribute to a cultural shift within the materials research community towards greater openness and collaboration. We are excited to be a part of this shift, and we look forward to seeing the innovative discoveries and breakthroughs that result from it. We are also grateful for the support provided to us by the National Science Foundation, which has enabled us to conduct this research and make our findings publicly available. We would like to extend our gratitude to the editorial team

Advanced composite materials with embedded fibers have numerous practical applications, and these materials' mechanical and electrical characteristics make them suitable for detecting damage through electrical methods. Due to the complex nature of composite materials, modeling their mechanical and electrical behavior is challenging, and existing models often require multiple material parameters that are difficult to obtain. This research focuses on developing a one-parameter model to describe the mechanical response and electrical conductivity of fiber-reinforced composites, incorporating the concept of internal state variables. By applying this model to a representative element method framework, we can simulate and study the behavior of composite materials under different loading conditions. Furthermore, we use this model to investigate a detection method for micro-cracks based on changes in electrical conductivity. This approach is then applied to a beam under various loading scenarios, demonstrating the capability to identify damage locations and sizes through electrical conductivity measurements. Notably, this method is shown to accurately detect small cracks that have not yet reached the size required for scattering, and it is also effective in distinguishing between different types of loading-induced damage. Overall, this research provides a theoretical foundation for using the developed model in a real-world application, such as developing a detection algorithm for experimental data. Ultimately, this work aims to lay the groundwork for a future detection algorithm that can be used in a real-time damage detection system. We've developed a computational model that simulates individual agents making choices based on their own and neighbors' past successes or failures. This simple decision-making process leads to the formation of distinct groups of winning and losing agents, mirroring a broader pattern observed in various real-world societies. Within this structure, we find that collective wisdom arises, specifically in how it allocates itself between different social layers. Our findings demonstrate that the emergence of collective wisdom is largely a result of individual intelligence, rather than resulting from complex interactions breaking it down, as some theories suggest. Instead, our model shows that even a small amount of individual intelligence can generate the kind of complex social hierarchy we observe in nature, and that this hierarchy is characterized by a specific mathematical property called scale-free behavior. By examining our model at the microscopic level, we gain insight into how individual intelligence influences decision-making, leading to the distribution of successes and failures that drive the formation of the complex social structure. Ultimately, our research reveals the fundamental connection between individual intelligence, decision-making, and complex social dynamics, and provides a framework for understanding the underlying mechanisms that give rise to the intricate patterns observed in natural societies. Our model's simplicity also makes its components easily identifiable, allowing us to extract general principles that can be applied to a wide range of complex systems found in various fields. Our results have implications for fields such as economics, biology, sociology, physics, and anthropology, and can be used to simulate and study the behavior of real-world societies, as well as provide a foundation for developing new decision-making strategies that take into account the complex social structures that often influence individual and collective outcomes. This work provides an analysis of tensor concepts within a Cartesian coordinate framework, offering a method to combine Euclidean space geometric principles with tensor calculus. Central to this approach is the identification of a specific mathematical structure in Euclidean space, which serves as a reference point for transforming tensors. A transformation rule specifically tailored for connecting different structures within Euclidean space is also established and shown to be equivalent to the conventional method of deriving tensor transformation rules using Jacobian matrices. The framework's versatility in accommodating curvilinear coordinate systems is demonstrated, along with the observation that gradient operators behave as covariant tensors in both Cartesian and curvilinear coordinates. The connection between the proposed approach and traditional methods involving Jacobian matrices and differential operators is explored, and the framework's applicability to the Dirac equation is demonstrated. The resulting formulation provides a coherent and self-consistent description of both classical and quantum mechanics. The developed framework also offers a pedagogical pathway for introducing advanced tensor-based formulations of fundamental physics to undergraduate-level students. The associated educational materials are available as part of the presented work. Toda conformal field theories are intricate systems that exhibit multiple mathematical structures, including Lie algebra and super-Lie algebra frameworks, and have been found to possess full W-symmetries in specific sectors. Notably, our research reveals the presence of full W$_2$-algebras in all sectors of the minimal series Toda conformal field theories. By examining the operator product expansion of W$_2$-algebras and the associated commutation relations, we have identified specific fields that generate these algebras and demonstrated how they can be used to derive the commutation relations of the original Lie algebra. Our findings are further supported by explicit computations of three-point functions involving W$_2$-algebra generators, and we have also established that the W$_2$-algebras reduce to W$_1$-algebras in the weak-coupling limit. Our work paves the way for exploring the relationship between Toda conformal field theories and the Kondo screening problem, as well as the study of the minimal series Toda theories in their thermodynamic limits. Our research also highlights the significance of W$_2$-algebras in understanding the properties of the W$_1$-algebras present in the Ramond sector of the minimal series Toda theories. Furthermore, our findings on the W$_2$-algebras provide the foundation for developing a Ramond sector analogue of the Ward-Boson construction, and we have outlined the necessary steps for achieving this goal in future studies. Recent advancements in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) aim to revive walking capabilities in spinal cord injury patients. Although these systems have shown promise in controlling virtual walkers and robotic legs, their effectiveness in actual physical therapy remains uncertain due to limited understanding of how they interact with muscles and the body. To address this, researchers have been using animal models to study BCIs in movement recovery. However, such studies have been limited to either sedated animals with impaired motor function or those that can walk normally. To address this limitation, a team of scientists has successfully implanted a BCI in rats with severe spinal cord injuries, allowing them to walk again. They used electrocorticography to track brain signals that control leg movements and a stimulator to apply electrical signals to the rats' muscles. By comparing the effects of BCIs on rats with varying levels of spinal cord damage, they found that those with more severe injuries required stronger brain signals to walk, but also showed greater muscle stimulation benefits. Furthermore, they discovered that BCIs could be used to relearn new walking patterns and that rats with spinal cord injuries could adapt to different types of muscle stimulation. To take their research further, the team developed a non-invasive method to record muscle activity and a computer program to control the stimulation based on the rats' brain signals and muscle activity. By studying the relationship between brain signals, muscle activity, and body movement, they found that the rats' gait patterns could be accurately predicted using just their brain signals. To demonstrate the practicality of their BCI design, the researchers successfully applied it to a real-world walking task, finding that it enabled the rats to walk further and with greater ease. To make their findings more applicable to humans, the team scaled up their BCI to match the human spinal cord and lower limbs, using a computer simulation to test it. This simulation revealed that their BCI could be used to revive walking in individuals with severe spinal cord injuries, allowing them to walk with the assistance of a walker. This breakthrough has significant implications for the treatment of spinal cord injuries and other neurological disorders that affect motor function. This leads to the conclusion that the associated $\Gamma$ has a non-trivial, minimal action on a linear tree if and only if every connected component of its graph is generated by an edge, thereby extending Guiraud's characterization to trees of any arity. Additionally, we show that any right-angled Artin group with a non-trivial action on a tree that is not a line has a subgroup whose image in its associated monoid acts transitively on an edge of the tree. Finally, we explore the relationship between these findings and the classical Burnside problem. These results were initially presented at the 2018 Geometry and Topology conference held in Minneapolis. In recent years, graph-based neural network methods have been highly effective, 
especially in processing complex data, however, these models are typically 
static and fail to capture the ever-changing graph structure that is prevalent 
in many real-world situations. This paper introduces a novel neural network called 
Temporal Graph Transformere (TGT), which is capable of learning transformations 
from input graphs and incorporates dynamic connectivity information. Unlike 
traditional graph neural networks, TGT employs a temporal attention mechanism to 
weigh the contributions of past representations and employs a spatial attention 
mechanism to focus on specific node relationships. Theoretical analysis of the 
learned representations reveals their connection to the graph's random walk information 
and learning transformations are treated as control problems. Experimental results 
on three datasets demonstrate TGT's superiority over static graph neural networks 
and alternative models, with improvements of up to 10.4% in accuracy. The code 
is publicly available at https://github.com/zhengzhengzhong1998/TGT. 

Based on the code and models, two additional applications were explored: 
one was a graph-to-graph sequence generation model that generated plausible 
telephone call graphs from input conversation texts, and the other was a node 
classification model that utilized a dynamic graph neural network to classify 
nodes in a molecular graph according to physical and chemical properties. The 
results showed that both models produced accurate and physically plausible graphs.
