This interconnection suggests a fundamental equivalence, which we can express as the notion that imperative algorithms essentially embody a form of proofs with cut operations. This equivalence serves as the foundation for an expanded framework, which we call "logical pseudocodes." Each statement in logical pseudocodes is analogous to a step in natural deduction, ensuring correctness and safety in accordance with the original specifications. This approach can be seen as a natural extension to the concept of algorithms, allowing us to derive logical pseudocodes from specifications and in the process gaining insight into the underlying logic. Furthermore, this method enables us to reconfigure our earlier system for proof search, known as "logical engines." This reconfiguration results in an enhanced understanding of how our previous system determines answers to queries, as seen in our prior work. As an added benefit, this new perspective simplifies the proof process for our logical engine, allowing it to accommodate more complex queries. Ultimately, this research framework offers a unique perspective on the relationship between algorithms and logical proofs, revealing that algorithms themselves can be viewed as a type of proof, with each step in the algorithm equivalent to a step in the proof. This discovery provides a compelling argument for the significance of this approach, given the inherent difficulties in verifying the correctness of algorithms, particularly given the rapid evolution of software. This challenge is further compounded by the growing reliance on complex software in critical applications. As a result, we believe that the concept of logical pseudocodes offers a promising solution to this challenge, with potential applications in the development of verifiable algorithms, as well as in areas such as proof theory, logic-based program synthesis, and formal methods for software development. We introduce a hierarchical model for large-scale discrete stochastic pursuit-evasion games, breaking down the strategy into multiple levels that account for variable dynamics, multiple agents, and uncertain environments. This framework enables the efficient solution of complex PEGs by focusing on a relatively small set of variables and exploiting recently developed fast solving methods for discrete stochastic optimal control. We then develop a hierarchical computation algorithm that leverages these methods and provides theoretical guarantees on its convergence and optimality. Furthermore, we establish bounds on the hierarchical solution's value function and show that it aligns with recent value function properties in PEGs. To illustrate the effectiveness of this approach, we apply it to a range of simulated scenarios involving multiple pursuers and obstacles. Additionally, we demonstrate the algorithm's performance in a real-world application using a drone as the pursuer. System and protocol level code for this example is also provided as part of the submission. We conclude by outlining potential future directions for this research, including potential extensions to continuous-time models and optimization techniques.

Due to the rise of forward radiation in the high-energy limit, lepton colliders with energies beyond a few TeV face significant challenges. As a result, the discovery potential for new physics beyond the standard model in certain scattering processes at the electron-positron collider is constrained. This study focuses on the $W^+W^-$ production at future lepton colliders and demonstrates that the kinematic range where the standard model is reliable can be expanded by utilizing the $W$-scalars, a novel beyond-standard-model scenario that deviates from conventional $W$-boson behavior. By introducing a suitable effective field theory and utilizing optimized cuts, we find that the $W^+W^-$ production at the 1 TeV electron-positron collider can be accurately understood within the standard model, leaving the true underlying explanation for the observed phenomenon to theories beyond the standard model. Furthermore, we find that the $W$-scalars, with masses in the TeV range, could potentially be discovered at the same collider via the $WW \to ZZ$ process at the 5$\sigma$ confidence level with an integrated luminosity of 1 inverse abbank. This research highlights the potential of the $WW \to ZZ$ process at future lepton colliders to uncover hidden physics in the $W$ sector. This work can be applied to other colliders, such as the International Linear Collider (ILC). This study also sheds light on the $e\gamma \to W^+W^-$ process at the future electron gamma colliders. This research can be further expanded to investigate other beyond-standard-model scenarios, such as the Higgs sector, by utilizing effective field theories. This approach can be used to investigate the $W^+W^-$ production at hadron colliders, such as the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can significantly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared value functions, our study
investigates the benefits of shared representations in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning. We introduce a centralized multi-task actor-critic model
that leverages a single, task-agnostic world model to learn from multiple
tasks. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using a single world model without
task identification does not yield performance gains over independent learning.
However, we demonstrate that by sharing a key component of the world model, the
intrinsic policy can exploit its structure to achieve improved results, thus
aligning with previous observations in model-free multi-task reinforcement learning.
Our approach is shown to be computationally efficient and capable of generalizing
to novel tasks with only minimal data, outperforming a baseline of independent
learning in several multi-task scenarios. Our code is publicly available at
\url{https://github.com/zhongyuyu1995/centralized_actor_critic}.

We synthesize Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem from 1931, along with Tarski's Undefinability Theorem from 1933, the Diagonal Lemma attributed to Godel-Carnap in 1934, and a strengthened form of the first incompleteness theorem by Rosser from 1936, whose respective proofs show striking similarities and utilize the same fundamental techniques. This analysis is made possible by adapting the language to be compatible with second-order arithmetic. We demonstrate that Godel's first incompleteness theorem can be derived from a combination of the other results, specifically using Tarski's undefinability theorem along with the Diagonal Lemma to obtain the kind of arithmetical diagonalization found in the first incompleteness theorem, and then further combining this with the properties of a consistent extension of Peano's arithmetic to obtain the strengthened form of the first incompleteness theorem by Rosser. This treatment also includes a discussion of the historical context of these theorems and their development over time. Additionally, we touch on some related topics and offer a few concluding remarks on their significance within the field of mathematical logic. This work is intended for readers who are already familiar with the fundamental concepts of mathematical logic but wish to gain a deeper understanding of these pivotal results and their historical development. This paper introduces a significant extension to the theory of functions u, subject to the equation ∆u = λu, within the framework of Clifford analysis. Specifically, we provide a proof of the Wiener-Hopf factorization for the kernel associated with ∆u = λu, thereby establishing the existence of an inverse operator for a class of functions that include this kernel. Our approach also yields an explicit formula for the square root of the Dirac Laplacian. Additionally, we derive the fundamental properties of this √∆ operator and its square root eigenvalue problem. Furthermore, our results can be applied to the study of a related PDE involving the Dirac operator, ∆_C. In solving inverse problems, researchers seek the most probable explanation for given data, by sampling and analyzing the associated posterior distribution. This approach is particularly valuable for addressing high-dimensional and nonlinear issues, as seen in recovering images from noisy measurements. Despite its benefits, posterior sampling can be computationally expensive, necessitating the development of efficient methods to extract key information from the posterior. One promising strategy involves leveraging the Wasserstein Transform, a flexible operational risk measure that can capture essential features of the posterior while meeting regulatory requirements. Theoretical and practical studies have demonstrated the efficacy of the Wasserstein Transform in capturing the posterior's most probable structure, even in challenging, high-dimensional settings. However, applying this method to large-scale inverse problems remains impractical due to the high computational cost of solving regularized optimization problems. To address this limitation, this work introduces a parallelizable and memory-efficient algorithm for solving a broad class of Eulerian operational risk measures, which encompasses the Wasserstein Transform as a special case. This efficient solver, under standard assumptions, provides a fast and accurate solution to large-scale problems, enabling the capture of posterior structure in high-dimensional inverse problems, even with massive-scale data. As a result, this method enables the seamless integration of the Wasserstein Transform and similar measures into large-scale inverse solving frameworks, facilitating the direct analysis of posterior distributions in high-dimensional settings. This is demonstrated through the reconstruction and analysis of MRI images from limited data, using a computational model that can be solved in parallel using a memory-efficient algorithm. This research was presented at the 2023 International Conference of the IEEE Engineering in Medicine and Biology Society.

This article examines the concept of invariant manifolds in dynamical systems from a stability perspective. We provide a review of theoretical frameworks for studying the behavior of systems with respect to invariant sets and manifolds, focusing on methods that account for disturbances and uncertainty. We then explore the application of these theories to specific systems, beginning with linear time-invariant models and progressing to nonlinear examples. Furthermore, we discuss the role of invariant sets in designing and analyzing control systems for achieving stability and meeting performance requirements. Alongside its relevance to mathematical analysis, we highlight the practical significance of understanding invariant patterns in experimental data. We also outline open research questions and potential avenues for future work on this topic. Despite the richness and diversity of its components, the field of dynamical systems benefits from a unified framework that highlights the central importance of invariant sets and manifolds. We anticipate this review will serve as a foundation for continued exploration and development within the community. We invite readers to contribute their insights and help us further refine our understanding of these fundamental concepts within the field of dynamical systems. The interstellar medium is home to scattering screens that can be studied by observing the periodic variations in the brightness of pulsars that shine through them. Pulsar PSR B1259-63 is an example of this phenomenon, exhibiting a peculiar behavior during its orbit around the Sco OB1 screen. While its primary emission is well-explained by a simple geometric model, there are remaining questions about the screen's properties, particularly how they change over time. To address this, a detailed analysis of 13 years' worth of data from very high-energy gamma-ray observations was conducted, and a new model that takes into account the screen's anisotropy and the pulsar's binary system was employed to study the phenomenon. According to the model, the screen's density peaks during the Australian summer, and it was found that the densities at both periastron and solstice are increasing over time, with rates of change of 0.3 percent per year for the peak density and 1 percent per year for the screen's free-electron density. Additionally, an analysis of the screen's temperature was performed, and it was discovered that the temperature is lower than expected, and it is rising at a rate of 0.03 Kelvin per year. The findings are consistent with the screen being shaped by a massive star that is surrounded by a massive disc, and it is proposed that future observations could reveal the arrival of a new relativistic population of particles as the pulsar approaches the periastron mark. The research was based on data collected from the Fermi Large Area Telescope. The study of the screen's properties over time also revealed a feature that was not anticipated, and it is suggested that it could be linked to the pulsar's interaction with the massive star's disc, and it is proposed that this phenomenon could be used as a tool for studying the properties of the star and its disc through relativistic particle physics. This paper introduces a new generative model called Pitch-Dilated ConvNet (PDC-Net), which generates high-fidelity audio waveforms at 24 kHz or 48 kHz. Pitch-Dilated ConvNet employs pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks to capture audio patterns across multiple time scales, achieving improved spectral representation and reduced spectral skewing. We further propose a novel adaptive duration predictor and a conditional vector generator to produce duration and conditioning vectors that enhance duration prediction and conditioning, respectively. Additionally, we introduce a spectral reshaper to rectify the frequency spectrum before waveform generation, resulting in cleaner waveforms and fewer mode collapses. Our model is scalable and we present two large-scale training datasets: one consisting of 10,000 hours of Western classical music and another of 1,000 hours of Chinese opera music. Our Pitch-Dilated ConvNet model achieves state-of-the-art results on both the Magnaea dataset at 24 kHz and the LJSpeech dataset at 48 kHz. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/paradiseJH/PDC-Net.

This bicategorical interpretation of THH is particularly relevant for commutative rings and polynomial rings. The underlying idea of shadows can be applied to a broad range of discrete functors, serving as a fundamental model for functors that can be described geometrically, and demonstrating preservation of Morita invariance. The resulting framework enables the derivation of shadow invariants for various functors, and facilitates the development of an axiomatic theory of THH equivalent to its classical definition, with additional features. These additional features include the ability to extend THH to functors that can be described geometrically, and reveal a connection to the concept of homotopy colimits. Our primary goal in this research is to pinpoint sound sources within video frames without relying on manually labeled data. To achieve this, a new end-to-end neural network for sound source localization is introduced, using a mixture density network to model probability distributions of feature points. To improve the network's performance and address the problem of focusing on difficult samples, we implemented a sample mining technique, labeling the most challenging examples as part of the unlabeled dataset. Our method involves assigning a weight to each unlabeled sample based on the uncertainty of the network, with greater weights given to more uncertain examples. As a result, the network is encouraged to concentrate on the most difficult samples and produce a probability distribution that covers a broader range of the input data. Our model was tested on two datasets – WildSound and USTC – and it outperformed the current state-of-the-art methods by a significant margin. Our code is available online. To the best of our knowledge, this research represents the first attempt at sound source localization without the use of labeled data. Our findings are particularly noteworthy given the challenges of this task and the absence of publicly accessible baselines for comparison. Our model's performance can be improved further by adjusting its hyperparameters and incorporating additional information from the video frames. Recent advancements in geometric neural networks have shown superior performance when using non-Euclidean geometry, specifically hyperbolic geometry, particularly in representing graphs with scale-free or hierarchical structures. Inspired by these findings, we introduce HGN, a general-purpose graph neural network based on hyperbolic geometry. By leveraging the hyperbolic distance metric and the spherical representation of learnable vectors in the embedding space, HGN achieves both interpretability and improved performance. We further investigate the impact of hyperbolic geometry's learning and embedding space's curvature, obtaining two key results. Firstly, we find that the optimal hyperbolic learning rate varies significantly across different tasks and models, and secondly, we discover that the choice of the spherical representation of vectors influences the model's performance. To facilitate further research and improve the effectiveness of HGN, we release our code and models publicly. Experimental evaluations on multiple datasets demonstrate HGN's superiority over existing graph neural networks. Furthermore, we observe that the model's performance can be enhanced by integrating a graph structure learning module, and we anticipate that future studies will explore this potential. This research examines how relative quantum cohomology evolves under certain mathematical transformations known as birational transformations, specifically within a particular class of complex geometric objects called toric complete intersections. Our findings reveal that the simplified quantum cohomology equations, which account for the effects of mathematical interactions between distinct objects, retain their same structure even after these transformations. Furthermore, we derive a formula that enables us to switch from the quantum cohomology of one object to that of another following Fano type birational transformations, analogous to how mathematical interactions between the two objects allow us to combine their quantum cohomology effects. Additionally, we explore and analyze specific cases of these transformations within two-dimensional spaces, providing visual representations of the resulting objects. Moreover, we demonstrate that within two-dimensional spaces, the resulting objects will always have the same mathematical properties as the original object, known as Del Pezzo surfaces, with the exception of one particular case. Notably, our research reveals that the quantum cohomology of the K3 surface associated with a given lattice is distinguishable from the quantum cohomology of an abelian surface, even after applying birational transformations, based on the configuration of the lattice. Lastly, we outline an approach to computing the quantum cohomology of the K3 surface associated with a given lattice, using the coordinates of the lattice rather than mathematical interactions between objects. This computation enables us to compare the quantum cohomology of the K3 surface with that of an abelian surface, highlighting the unique features of the K3 surface. In this research, we utilize a transfer learning approach to apply the technique on low-dose chest X-rays, enhancing their quality to match that of high-dose images. Our contributions are as follows: we introduce a new metric to assess the realism of synthetic images in comparison to their corresponding reference images; we develop a chest X-ray image enhancement model using U-Net architecture and a GAN-based conditional text-to-image model; we conduct multiple experiments to evaluate the performance of our model, including a study on the optimal learning rate, a comparison with a baseline model, and an analysis of our newly proposed metric. Our results demonstrate that this technique enhances the quality of low-dose chest X-rays to match high-dose standards, as evaluated by a human expert.
